Class #1 · Overview of financial accounting (9 Oct.)

Why financial accounting matters

  • Accounting is the "language of business". Financial accounting reports the resources a company controls and how management uses them.
  • Users: shareholders, lenders, suppliers, customers, employees, analysts, the State, the public, management. Information that meets investors' needs is assumed to meet everyone's.
  • This course takes the user's perspective: read and interpret financial statements.

Key concepts · The business equation

Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' equity Net income = Revenue - Expenses (net income stays inside equity)
TermCourse definition (IASB 2018 conceptual framework)
AssetA present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events; an economic resource is a right that has the potential to produce economic benefits. Current or non-current.
LiabilityA present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events. Current or non-current.
Shareholders' equityThe residual interest in the assets after deducting liabilities: share capital + retained earnings.
RevenueAn increase in assets or decrease in liabilities that increases equity, excluding shareholders' contributions.
ExpenseA decrease in assets or increase in liabilities that decreases equity, excluding distributions to shareholders.

Mechanism · How every transaction keeps the equation balanced

  1. Identify what the company receives and what it gives up or owes.
  2. Every transaction either changes both sides by the same amount (+X / +X or -X / -X) or reclassifies within one side (+X and -X).
  3. Then ask: does it touch shareholders' equity? If yes, it is revenue or an expense - unless it is a shareholders' contribution or a dividend.
Net income is not cash. Some transactions move cash without touching income (borrowing, buying equipment, repaying a loan); others hit income and cash in different periods (credit sales, credit purchases). That is the accruals principle.

The financial statements

  • Statement of financial position (balance sheet): uses of resources (assets) and their origins (liabilities and equity) at a point in time.
  • Income statement (statement of profit or loss): revenue - expenses over the period.
  • Statement of changes in equity, statement of cash flows (operating, investing, financing) and notes.
  • The statements are linked: net income feeds equity; the change in cash explains the cash line of the balance sheet.

The rules of the game

  • Why rules: to value assets and liabilities, recognize revenue and expenses, and separate an asset from an expense (a share bought for 5 worth 30 at year-end; a pool table sold on 31/12, delivered on 31/01; 60M of R&D).
  • Standard setters: the IASB (IAS/IFRS) and the ISSB (sustainability, IFRS S1 and S2, since 2021) within the IFRS Foundation; the EU ("IFRS as adopted by the EU"); the FASB (US GAAP); the ANC (French rules). US GAAP is more rules-based, IFRS more principles-based. The 1993 Daimler-Benz example: a profit of 615M DM under German rules, a loss of 1,839M DM under US GAAP.
  • Principles: going concern, faithful representation (complete, neutral, free from error), consistency, accruals, prudence, monetary unit.
  • Measurement bases: historical cost (easy, verifiable, but blind to market value) and current value, including fair value (market price; mostly financial instruments; IAS 16 allows revaluation, IAS 40 fair value for investment property).
  • Governance: shareholders elect the board, which appoints management and an audit committee; the auditor certifies the accounts.
2027 change (IFRS 18). IFRS 18 replaces IAS 1 for periods starting on or after 1 January 2027. The income statement is split into five categories (operating, investing, financing, tax, discontinued operations) with two subtotals: operating profit and profit before financing and tax. This course presents the 2026 statements.

Classic traps

  • Collecting a receivable or paying a payable does not touch income.
  • A loan is not revenue; repaying it is not an expense; only the interest is an expense.
  • A shareholders' contribution increases equity without being revenue.

Class #2 · Operating cycle and current assets (16 Oct.)

Key concepts · The operating cycle

Purchases → inventories → production → sales → receivables → collections; purchases → payables → payments. Current assets are used within one cycle and turn into cash within a year: inventories, trade receivables, tax receivables, advances to suppliers, cash.

Mechanism · Recognizing revenue and expenses

Accrual accountingCash accounting
RevenueWhen the performance obligation is satisfied (at a point in time or over time)When collected
ExpensesWhen incurredWhen paid
  1. IFRS 15 five-step model: identify the contract; identify the performance obligations; determine the transaction price; allocate it to the obligations; recognize revenue when (or as) each obligation is satisfied.
  2. Goods: at a point in time (transfer of control); services: over time. LVMH example: retail sales recognized when the customer buys, services as rendered, net of discounts.
  3. The ideal is to match expenses to the revenue they helped produce.
Revenue recognition is the fraud hotspot. In 60% of the US scandals studied by COSO, revenue recognition was manipulated: period shifts ("cookie jar") or fictitious sales (Gowex, Satyam). See also Tesco (2014).

Inventories

  • Until a product is sold, its costs stay on the balance sheet. Measured at the lower of cost and net realizable value.
  • Types: merchandise, raw materials, finished goods.
Acquisition cost = purchase price + costs to bring the inventory on site and to condition (transport, handling) + directly attributable costs (customs, non-recoverable taxes) - discounts Production cost = direct costs + a systematic share of production overheads Cost of goods sold = opening inventory + purchases - closing inventory
MethodAssumptionEffect
Specific identificationNon-fungible goodsActual cost of each item
FIFOFirst in, first outClosing inventory near recent prices (balance-sheet oriented)
LIFOLast in, first outBanned under IFRS, allowed under US GAAP; reacts fast to prices (income-statement oriented)
WACWeighted average cost, recomputed at each purchaseNo assumed order

Worked example · Case Cameras (official)

Cameras · WAC vs FIFO vs LIFO Class #2 slidesOfficial solution

Opening inventory 1 Jan: 50 cameras at 100 euros. 10/01: buy 75 at 110. 15/01: sell 60 at 150. 20/01: buy 25 at 120. 30/01: sell 40 at 150. Closing inventory and impact under each method?

See the official solution

WAC: on 15/01 the average is (50×100 + 75×110)/125 = 106 → COGS 60×106 = 6,360, inventory 65×106 = 6,890. On 30/01: (65×106 + 25×120)/90 = 109.9 → COGS 40×109.9 = 4,396; closing inventory 50×109.9 = 5,495.

FIFO: on 15/01 out go 50×100 + 10×110 = 6,100; on 30/01 out go 40×110 = 4,400; closing inventory 25×110 + 25×120 = 5,750.

LIFO: on 15/01 out go 60×110 = 6,600; on 30/01 out go 25×120 + 15×110 = 4,650; closing inventory 50×100 = 5,000.

FIFOWACLIFO
Sales15,00015,00015,000
COGS10,50010,75611,250
Profit4,5004,2443,750
Closing inventory5,7505,4955,000
When prices rise, FIFO maximizes profit and closing inventory and minimizes COGS; LIFO does the opposite. When prices fall, the effects reverse.

Accounts receivable

  • They exist because transactions are not settled instantly and accounting is accrual-based.
  • Doubtful receivable: an allowance on the balance sheet, with an expense in the income statement. Uncollectible receivable: written off, with a loss. Under IFRS 9 (simplified approach), trade receivables are impaired from day one for lifetime expected credit losses.

Class #3 · Investing cycle and non-current assets (23 Oct.)

Key concepts · Current vs non-current

  • A non-current asset is not meant to be turned into cash within the normal cycle (usually one year). The difference with a current asset is use: the same car is a fixed asset for one company and inventory for a car dealer.
TypeExamplesConsumption
Property, plant & equipmentBuildings, equipment, machinesDepreciation
LandNo depreciation
Natural resourcesDeposits, quarriesDepletion
Finite-life intangiblesPatents, software, licences, franchisesAmortization
Indefinite-life intangiblesBrands, goodwillNo amortization (impairment tests)
Financial assetsSecurities, long-term loansNo amortization; amortized cost or fair value (IFRS 9)

Mechanism · Initial recognition at cost

  1. Start from the acquisition cost (if bought) or production cost (if built).
  2. Add the directly attributable costs needed to bring the asset to working condition: site preparation, delivery, installation, architects' and engineers' fees, estimated dismantling costs.
  3. Slide example: price 100 + customs 5 + transport 15 + fees 30 = equipment at 150.
  • Intangibles: identifiable non-monetary assets without physical substance, recognized if future benefits are probable and the cost is measurable (e.g. development costs). No asset for internally generated brands, internal goodwill, customer lists, advertising, training or research. Only acquired goodwill is recognized (price paid - fair value of net identifiable assets; LVMH and Tiffany in 2021).

Mechanism · Depreciation

Depreciable amount = cost - residual value Straight-line: rate = 1 / useful life; annual charge = depreciable amount x rate Declining balance (DDBM): rate = 2 x straight-line rate; charge = net book value x rate Net book value = cost - accumulated depreciation (- impairment) Gain or loss on disposal = sale price - net book value
  • Partial year: pro-rate the charge (months or days).
  • Accelerated methods charge more in early years (cars, ovens) and bring a tax shield. In the US the multiple is often 2; in continental Europe the tax authorities set coefficients by useful life.

Worked example · Straight-line and declining balance (official)

Two depreciation schedules Class #3 slidesOfficial solution

(1) Cost 11,000, residual value 1,000, 5 years, straight-line. (2) NCA machine of 15,000 over 10 years, double declining balance: charges for the first two years.

See the official solution

X12,0002,0009,000
X22,0004,0007,000
X32,0006,0005,000
X42,0008,0003,000
X52,00010,0001,000

(1) Depreciable amount 10,000 × 20% = 2,000 per year. (2) Straight-line rate 10% → DDBM 20%. Year 1: 15,000 × 20% = 3,000 (NBV 12,000). Year 2: 12,000 × 20% = 2,400; cumulated 5,400; NBV 9,600.

Derecognition

On disposal, or when no future benefit is expected: remove the net book value and recognize the net result of the sale (IAS 16.68). Slide example: equipment with an NBV of 40M sold for 45M → gain of 5M.

Depreciation is an expense with no cash effect (except through tax). Book value is usually not market value: hidden gains can exist. Always challenge the assumptions (useful life, pattern of consumption).

Class #4 · Financing cycle, equity and liabilities (30 Oct.)

Key concepts · Equity vocabulary

Share capital = number of shares x par value Book value per share = shareholders' equity / number of shares Market capitalization = number of shares x share price Share premium = (issue price - par value) x new shares issued
  • Par value only defines the number of shares in the legal capital and each shareholder's power. Par ≠ book value ≠ market value.
  • The share premium (additional paid-in capital, capital surplus) records what new shareholders pay above the legal capital; it belongs to equity.

Mechanism · Issuing new shares

  1. New shares x par value → increases share capital.
  2. New shares x (issue price - par value) → increases share premium.
  3. New shares x issue price → cash coming in.

Profit appropriation

  • Three destinations: reserves (legal, statutory, free), dividends, retained earnings.
  • Three cases: keep everything in reserves, distribute everything, or a mix. Dividends decided but not yet paid become a liability (dividends payable).
  • The balance sheet is presented before appropriation (the year's income on its own line) or after (reserves updated, dividends in liabilities).

Liabilities

A liability is a present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of a past event (legally enforceable or customarily accepted; settled in cash, goods, services, shares…).

Debt vs equity

DebtEquity
RepaymentMandatoryNone
FlexibilityHigh (term, amount, refinancing)Low, high transaction costs, irreversible decision
CostInterest due whatever the income, market rateNo mandatory return; dividends if profits; higher expected return (risk)
TaxInterest usually deductibleDividends usually not deductible
PowerNo control over managementInfluence and control; dilution with new shareholders
Use of fundsCan be tied to a project (guarantees, mortgages)Not earmarked
Debt and equity play different risk/reward roles. Some companies have only private equity yet issue public debt (bonds). Analysts, shareholders and creditors all read this split.

Class #5 · End-of-Year adjustments (6 Nov.)

Why year-end adjustments

Depreciation and impairment, accruals and deferrals, provisions, doubtful receivables: they apply the accruals, matching and prudence principles, cutting activity into annual periods at the closing date (often 31 December). The slides show a company can be very profitable with dangerously low cash (clients paying at two months, suppliers at one), or loss-making with rising cash.

Mechanism · Accruals and deferrals

SituationCashExpense / revenueClosing entry
Prepaid expensePaid in NRelates to N+1Asset "prepaid expense"; reduce the expense of N
Deferred revenueCollected in NRelates to N+1Liability "deferred revenue"; reduce the revenue of N
Accrued expensePaid in N+1Relates to NLiability "accrued expense"; expense of N
Accrued revenueCollected in N+1Relates to NAsset "accrued revenue"; revenue of N
Slide exampleEntry at 31/12/N
Rent of 9,000 paid on 01/11/N for Nov, Dec and JanPrepaid expense +3,000; expense of N = 6,000
December electricity bill of 100, received and paid on 05/01/N+1Accrued expense +100; expense of N = 100
Annual subscription of 1,200 collected on 01/07/N, all in revenueDeferred revenue +600; revenue of N = 600
Invoice of 900 issued on 01/02/N+1 for Nov, Dec and JanAccrued revenue +600; revenue of N = 600

Mechanism · Impairment of assets

Recoverable amount = max(fair value - costs of disposal; value in use) Impairment loss = carrying amount - recoverable amount (if positive)
  • Prudence: an asset may not sit on the books above its recoverable amount. Value in use = present value of the asset's expected cash flows.
  • One-off test, usually at closing. Reversal allowed if the recoverable amount rises again (IAS 36.114), capped at what the carrying amount would have been without impairment; never for goodwill.

Provisions

CauseTimingAmount
Certain liabilityReal and presentCertainCertain
Accrued expenseReal and presentNear certainUncertain
ProvisionReal and presentUncertainUncertain
Contingent liabilityPossible obligation, or present but unrecognizedUncertainUncertain
  • A provision is a liability of uncertain timing or amount. Three cumulative conditions: a present obligation (legal or constructive) from a past event; a probable outflow of resources; a reliable estimate. Otherwise no provision, only a contingent liability disclosed in the notes.
  • Accounting: an expense and a provision in liabilities, at the best estimate. Later: use (liability and cash both fall) or reversal (liability falls, revenue is recognized).
Slide caseProvision?
Shop that refunds unhappy customers under a well-known policy, no legal obligationYes: constructive obligation, if outflow probable and estimable
Oil company polluting in a country with no law; clean-up law near certain just after the 20X0 closingNo in earlier years; yes in 20X0 because of the new law
Division closure decided on 12/12, not announced nor startedNo: the obligation arises from the announcement
Warranty: 75% no defect, 20% small defect (1), 5% large defect (10), 10,000 productsYes: 10,000×20%×1 + 10,000×5%×10 = 7,000
Food poisoning after a wedding: loss improbable in 20X0, probable in 20X120X0: contingent liability; 20X1: provision
Forbidden: provisions for future operating losses. Restructuring: only with a detailed formal plan, already started or announced to those affected. Accruals are meant to cut off annual periods, so their cash implications are (very) different, and they create opportunities for earnings manipulation that analysts watch closely.

Class #6 · Statement of cash flows (13 Nov.)

Key concept · What the statement explains

The statement of cash flows explains the change in cash and cash equivalents (very liquid short-term investments with negligible risk of value change) over the period.

Operating cash flows (I) + Investing cash flows (II) = investment inflows - outflows + Financing cash flows (III) = financing inflows - outflows = Net change in cash (IV) Closing cash = opening cash + IV

The three activities

ActivityInflowsOutflows
OperatingSales of goods and services, royalties, commissionsPurchases, wages and social charges, taxes
InvestingDisposals of fixed assets, repayments of loans grantedPurchases of fixed assets, loans granted, securities (not cash equivalents)
FinancingShare issues, borrowingsShare buybacks, loan repayments
Interest and dividends. Until 2026 (IAS 7), a choice: interest and dividends received in operating or investing; paid in operating or financing; tax in operating. From 1 January 2027 (IAS 7 amended by IFRS 18), for most entities: received in investing, paid in financing, tax in operating. In the exam, read the classification instructions.

Mechanism · Direct and indirect methods

  • Direct: collections from customers minus payments to suppliers, employees, etc. (from actual cash movements).
  • Indirect: start from net income and correct it. A semi-direct variant corrects sales by the change in receivables, etc. Both methods give the same figure and concern only operating flows.
  • From 2027, the indirect method starts from operating profit.
Indirect method: Net income + depreciation, amortization and impairment charges, - reversals (non-cash items) - gains / + losses on disposals (remove disposal results) - increase in inventories and receivables (+ if decrease) + increase in trade and operating payables (- if decrease) = Operating cash flow

Worked example · Verdi's statement of cash flows (official)

Verdi, year X1 Class #6 / #1 slidesOfficial solution
Cash received from clients+180
Cash paid to suppliers-80
Cash paid to employees-101
Operating cash flow-1
Purchase of equipment-125
Investing cash flow-125
Proceeds from share issue / bank loan+150 / +60
Repayment of bank loan / interest paid-12 / -4
Financing cash flow+194
Opening 0 → closing cash68

Reading the statement

  • Operating flows: normally positive. Investing: generally negative (positive after a big disposal). Financing: positive or negative depending on the first two.
  • Related transactions land in different sections: paying for inventory reduces operating flows; paying for a machine reduces investing flows.
  • "Cash is king", but the statement does not tell the whole story.

Class #7 · Introduction to Management Accounting; costing terms and purpose (20 Nov.)

Key concepts · What management accounting is

  • It measures and communicates financial and non-financial information to help managers decide (launch a product, accept a client, make or buy…) and shape strategy (cost leadership or differentiation).
  • Financial accounting: record, report outside, mandatory and standardized, annual, historical. Management accounting: specific to each organization, not mandatory, forward-looking, at any frequency (month, week, ad hoc). Management control uses this information to steer strategy and operations (budgets, variances, performance measurement).

Cost terms

  • Cost: a resource sacrificed to reach a goal. Cost object: anything whose cost we want to measure (brand, range, client, project, activity…).
  • Not all costs are expenses and vice versa: an investment is neither (cash down, asset up); depreciation is both a cost and an expense with no cash outflow.
DistinctionDefinitionKeep in mind
Variable / fixedVariable: varies in total with volume. Fixed: does not vary in total over the period despite volume.Depends on the contract and the horizon: the longer the horizon, the more costs are variable.
Direct / indirectDirect: traceable to the cost object in an economically feasible way. Indirect: linked to the object but not traceable; must be allocated.Depends on the cost object, the materiality of the cost, data collection technology, the organization.
Use unit costs cautiously. Unit cost = total cost / number of units. Kruger: fixed rent 94,500 + handlebar 52 per bike. At 1,000 bikes: (94,500 + 52,000)/1,000 = 146.50. At 600 bikes: (94,500 + 31,200)/600 = 209.50. Using 146.50 would understate the cost.

Mechanism · The cost-volume-profit (CVP) model

Profit = P x Q - v x Q - FC Contribution margin per unit = P - v Contribution margin ratio = (P - v) / P Breakeven volume = FC / (P - v) Breakeven revenue = FC / margin ratio Volume for a target profit = (FC + target profit) / (P - v) Margin of safety = sales - breakeven sales
  • Assumptions: volume is the only driver; costs split into fixed and variable, linear within the relevant range; price, unit costs and fixed costs known and constant; one product or a constant mix; no time value of money.
  • Uses: business plans, feasibility, profitability and risk diagnosis. Limits: single driver, linearity, constant mix, the fixed/variable split depends on the horizon.

Worked example · Dresses by Mary (official)

CVP and an advertising decision Class #7 slidesOfficial solution

Purchase 32 + other variable costs 10 per dress, price 70, fixed costs 84,000. Contribution per unit 28 (ratio 40%). At 2,500 dresses: 175,000 - 105,000 - 84,000 = -14,000. Breakeven: 84,000/28 = 3,000 dresses. An advertising campaign of 10,000 lifts sales from 3,200 to 4,000: profit goes from 5,600 to 18,000, i.e. +12,400 → run the campaign.

Relevant costs for decisions

  • Relevant costs and revenues: future costs and revenues that differ between options. Historical costs only help forecast; sunk costs are irrelevant.
  • Do not assume all variable costs are relevant, nor that all fixed costs are irrelevant. Full unit costs can mislead (irrelevant costs included; same unit cost at different volumes).
  • Opportunity cost: the contribution given up by not using a limited resource in its best alternative use; never recorded in accounting.
  • Scarce resource: at full capacity, rank products by contribution per unit of the scarce resource, not per unit of product.
  • Pricing: cost is only one input (competition, clients' ability to pay, perceived value); separate special sales from the regular price.
Noel (towels): capacity 44,000, production 30,000; variable 8.50 (6.50 + 0.50 + 1.50); fixed 150,000. Full cost (8.5×30,000 + 150,000)/30,000 = 13.50. A special order of 5,000 at 11.50: only variable costs change → contribution 3 × 5,000 = +15,000, accept (spare capacity exists).
Tiilikainen: motorbike engine, contribution 240 for 2h; boat engine, 375 for 5h; 600h available. Contribution per hour 120 vs 75 → favor motorbike engines.

Class #8 · Cost allocation: job order costing and process-costing (27 Nov.)

Why allocate indirect costs

  • Direct costs are traced; indirect costs are shared resources that must be allocated to build a full cost (pricing, portfolio strategy, cost reduction, full-cost inventory valuation).
Careful: never use a full cost to drop a product or outsource - reason with differential costs and revenues instead.

Key concepts

Full cost = traced direct costs + allocated indirect costs Cost per allocation unit = cost pool total / number of units of the allocation base Indirect cost charged = units consumed x cost per allocation unit
  • Cost pool: a grouping of indirect costs. Allocation base (cost driver, unite d'oeuvre): a measurable variable (hours, kg, euros, m2…) causally linked to the pool's costs. A homogeneous pool gathers costs with the same cause.
  • Choosing the driver: economic plausibility, quality of fit, regression slope.
  • Support pools (IT, HR, R&D, maintenance) vs operating pools (purchasing, production, distribution).

Job costing and process costing

ServicesManufacturing
Job costing (cost per order, batch or mission)Audit, consulting, ad campaignAircraft assembly, house building
Process costing (average cost of identical units)Deposit processing, standard mailRefining, food processing

Job-costing steps: identify the job; its direct costs; the relevant indirect pools; each pool's allocation base; the cost per allocation unit; then charge the job.

Mechanism · Allocating support pools

  1. Direct method: only services to operating pools count (simplest, most used).
  2. Step-down method: allocate first the support pool that serves the other support pools the most, then the next, with no return.
  3. Reciprocal method: all cross-services (equations); off syllabus. The French "centres d'analyse" method (PCG 1947) uses it.

The method chosen changes the relative cost of products, and therefore performance evaluation. The cost of a product is a construct: always state the purpose, the context and the conventions.

Class #9 · Activity-Based Costing (4 Dec.)

Key concepts · Why ABC

  • Born in the US in the 1980s, when a single cost pool was no longer enough. Pools are multiplied to stay homogeneous and split by activities rather than by organizational departments.
  • No more support vs operating pools: every activity is charged to cost objects according to its consumption of drivers.

Mechanism · Implementing ABC

  1. Define the cost objects; (2) their direct costs; (3) the activities, their costs and their driver; compute the cost per driver; (4) charge according to driver consumption.
Cost per driver = activity cost / total number of drivers Cost charged to a product = Sum(drivers consumed x cost per driver)

Strengths and limits

  • Strengths: faithful modeling (especially of complexity: number of products, components), traceability, well suited to services and processes.
  • Limits: a heavy database (drivers x products) to build and maintain, risk of bureaucracy.
  • From ABC to ABM (activity-based management): cut costs, improve processes, plan activities, set prices and mix, think about customer value. About 40% of US companies use ABC, 20-35% in Europe and France.
Cutting the number of drivers of a product changes the split between products, not necessarily the company's total cost.
Class #10 · Introduction to budget and variance analysis (11 Dec.)

Key concepts · What a budget is

  • A quantified expression, over a limited period (usually one year), of a forward-looking view of the company, with financial and non-financial items. A reference point for action. Master budget and departmental budgets; no standard template; most are built on a projected income statement.
  • Approach: strategy → objectives → action plans → resources, from past performance and forecasts.
  • It sits in a wider process: strategic plan (3-5 years), capital budgets, operational plans (1-3 years), annual budget, departmental budgets (sales, production, materials, labor, overheads, cash, financing).

Common problems and control

  • Imposed without managers, a budget looks unrealistic and is little used; built with them, it takes time and triggers negotiations.
  • Control: compare budget and actual, adjust forecasts; this is the pivot of performance and variance analysis.

Mechanism · Variance analysis (sample exam "A la Coque")

Flexible budget = budget recomputed at the actual volume, with budgeted prices and unit costs Total (static budget) variance = actual - static budget Volume variance = flexible budget - static budget Flexible budget variance = actual - flexible budget A variance is favorable if it increases profit
The slides note that variance analysis was not covered in class, but it appears in a sample paper (A la Coque): know at least these three formulas.

Course wrap-up

Across Class #7-#10 you covered: the financial accounting / management accounting / control articulation; cost terms and their uses; decision-making with the CVP model; cost allocation methods (direct, step-down, ABC); and budgeting. Management accounting deals with information about the acquisition and consumption of resources, to make managers' decisions easier.

Class #1 · Overview of financial accounting (9 Oct.)

Why financial accounting matters

  • Accounting is the "language of business". Financial accounting reports the resources a company controls and how management uses them.
  • Users: shareholders, lenders, suppliers, customers, employees, analysts, the State, the public, management. Information that meets investors' needs is assumed to meet everyone's.
  • This course takes the user's perspective: read and interpret financial statements.

Key concepts · The business equation

Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' equity Net income = Revenue - Expenses (net income stays inside equity)
TermCourse definition (IASB 2018 conceptual framework)
AssetA present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events; an economic resource is a right that has the potential to produce economic benefits. Current or non-current.
LiabilityA present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events. Current or non-current.
Shareholders' equityThe residual interest in the assets after deducting liabilities: share capital + retained earnings.
RevenueAn increase in assets or decrease in liabilities that increases equity, excluding shareholders' contributions.
ExpenseA decrease in assets or increase in liabilities that decreases equity, excluding distributions to shareholders.

Mechanism · How every transaction keeps the equation balanced

  1. Identify what the company receives and what it gives up or owes.
  2. Every transaction either changes both sides by the same amount (+X / +X or -X / -X) or reclassifies within one side (+X and -X).
  3. Then ask: does it touch shareholders' equity? If yes, it is revenue or an expense - unless it is a shareholders' contribution or a dividend.
Net income is not cash. Some transactions move cash without touching income (borrowing, buying equipment, repaying a loan); others hit income and cash in different periods (credit sales, credit purchases). That is the accruals principle.

The financial statements

  • Statement of financial position (balance sheet): uses of resources (assets) and their origins (liabilities and equity) at a point in time.
  • Income statement (statement of profit or loss): revenue - expenses over the period.
  • Statement of changes in equity, statement of cash flows (operating, investing, financing) and notes.
  • The statements are linked: net income feeds equity; the change in cash explains the cash line of the balance sheet.

The rules of the game

  • Why rules: to value assets and liabilities, recognize revenue and expenses, and separate an asset from an expense (a share bought for 5 worth 30 at year-end; a pool table sold on 31/12, delivered on 31/01; 60M of R&D).
  • Standard setters: the IASB (IAS/IFRS) and the ISSB (sustainability, IFRS S1 and S2, since 2021) within the IFRS Foundation; the EU ("IFRS as adopted by the EU"); the FASB (US GAAP); the ANC (French rules). US GAAP is more rules-based, IFRS more principles-based. The 1993 Daimler-Benz example: a profit of 615M DM under German rules, a loss of 1,839M DM under US GAAP.
  • Principles: going concern, faithful representation (complete, neutral, free from error), consistency, accruals, prudence, monetary unit.
  • Measurement bases: historical cost (easy, verifiable, but blind to market value) and current value, including fair value (market price; mostly financial instruments; IAS 16 allows revaluation, IAS 40 fair value for investment property).
  • Governance: shareholders elect the board, which appoints management and an audit committee; the auditor certifies the accounts.
2027 change (IFRS 18). IFRS 18 replaces IAS 1 for periods starting on or after 1 January 2027. The income statement is split into five categories (operating, investing, financing, tax, discontinued operations) with two subtotals: operating profit and profit before financing and tax. This course presents the 2026 statements.

Classic traps

  • Collecting a receivable or paying a payable does not touch income.
  • A loan is not revenue; repaying it is not an expense; only the interest is an expense.
  • A shareholders' contribution increases equity without being revenue.

Class #2 · Operating cycle and current assets (16 Oct.)

Key concepts · The operating cycle

Purchases → inventories → production → sales → receivables → collections; purchases → payables → payments. Current assets are used within one cycle and turn into cash within a year: inventories, trade receivables, tax receivables, advances to suppliers, cash.

Mechanism · Recognizing revenue and expenses

Accrual accountingCash accounting
RevenueWhen the performance obligation is satisfied (at a point in time or over time)When collected
ExpensesWhen incurredWhen paid
  1. IFRS 15 five-step model: identify the contract; identify the performance obligations; determine the transaction price; allocate it to the obligations; recognize revenue when (or as) each obligation is satisfied.
  2. Goods: at a point in time (transfer of control); services: over time. LVMH example: retail sales recognized when the customer buys, services as rendered, net of discounts.
  3. The ideal is to match expenses to the revenue they helped produce.
Revenue recognition is the fraud hotspot. In 60% of the US scandals studied by COSO, revenue recognition was manipulated: period shifts ("cookie jar") or fictitious sales (Gowex, Satyam). See also Tesco (2014).

Inventories

  • Until a product is sold, its costs stay on the balance sheet. Measured at the lower of cost and net realizable value.
  • Types: merchandise, raw materials, finished goods.
Acquisition cost = purchase price + costs to bring the inventory on site and to condition (transport, handling) + directly attributable costs (customs, non-recoverable taxes) - discounts Production cost = direct costs + a systematic share of production overheads Cost of goods sold = opening inventory + purchases - closing inventory
MethodAssumptionEffect
Specific identificationNon-fungible goodsActual cost of each item
FIFOFirst in, first outClosing inventory near recent prices (balance-sheet oriented)
LIFOLast in, first outBanned under IFRS, allowed under US GAAP; reacts fast to prices (income-statement oriented)
WACWeighted average cost, recomputed at each purchaseNo assumed order

Accounts receivable

  • They exist because transactions are not settled instantly and accounting is accrual-based.
  • Doubtful receivable: an allowance on the balance sheet, with an expense in the income statement. Uncollectible receivable: written off, with a loss. Under IFRS 9 (simplified approach), trade receivables are impaired from day one for lifetime expected credit losses.

Class #3 · Investing cycle and non-current assets (23 Oct.)

Key concepts · Current vs non-current

  • A non-current asset is not meant to be turned into cash within the normal cycle (usually one year). The difference with a current asset is use: the same car is a fixed asset for one company and inventory for a car dealer.
TypeExamplesConsumption
Property, plant & equipmentBuildings, equipment, machinesDepreciation
LandNo depreciation
Natural resourcesDeposits, quarriesDepletion
Finite-life intangiblesPatents, software, licences, franchisesAmortization
Indefinite-life intangiblesBrands, goodwillNo amortization (impairment tests)
Financial assetsSecurities, long-term loansNo amortization; amortized cost or fair value (IFRS 9)

Mechanism · Initial recognition at cost

  1. Start from the acquisition cost (if bought) or production cost (if built).
  2. Add the directly attributable costs needed to bring the asset to working condition: site preparation, delivery, installation, architects' and engineers' fees, estimated dismantling costs.
  3. Slide example: price 100 + customs 5 + transport 15 + fees 30 = equipment at 150.
  • Intangibles: identifiable non-monetary assets without physical substance, recognized if future benefits are probable and the cost is measurable (e.g. development costs). No asset for internally generated brands, internal goodwill, customer lists, advertising, training or research. Only acquired goodwill is recognized (price paid - fair value of net identifiable assets; LVMH and Tiffany in 2021).

Mechanism · Depreciation

Depreciable amount = cost - residual value Straight-line: rate = 1 / useful life; annual charge = depreciable amount x rate Declining balance (DDBM): rate = 2 x straight-line rate; charge = net book value x rate Net book value = cost - accumulated depreciation (- impairment) Gain or loss on disposal = sale price - net book value
  • Partial year: pro-rate the charge (months or days).
  • Accelerated methods charge more in early years (cars, ovens) and bring a tax shield. In the US the multiple is often 2; in continental Europe the tax authorities set coefficients by useful life.

Derecognition

On disposal, or when no future benefit is expected: remove the net book value and recognize the net result of the sale (IAS 16.68). Slide example: equipment with an NBV of 40M sold for 45M → gain of 5M.

Depreciation is an expense with no cash effect (except through tax). Book value is usually not market value: hidden gains can exist. Always challenge the assumptions (useful life, pattern of consumption).

Class #4 · Financing cycle, equity and liabilities (30 Oct.)

Key concepts · Equity vocabulary

Share capital = number of shares x par value Book value per share = shareholders' equity / number of shares Market capitalization = number of shares x share price Share premium = (issue price - par value) x new shares issued
  • Par value only defines the number of shares in the legal capital and each shareholder's power. Par ≠ book value ≠ market value.
  • The share premium (additional paid-in capital, capital surplus) records what new shareholders pay above the legal capital; it belongs to equity.

Mechanism · Issuing new shares

  1. New shares x par value → increases share capital.
  2. New shares x (issue price - par value) → increases share premium.
  3. New shares x issue price → cash coming in.

Profit appropriation

  • Three destinations: reserves (legal, statutory, free), dividends, retained earnings.
  • Three cases: keep everything in reserves, distribute everything, or a mix. Dividends decided but not yet paid become a liability (dividends payable).
  • The balance sheet is presented before appropriation (the year's income on its own line) or after (reserves updated, dividends in liabilities).

Liabilities

A liability is a present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of a past event (legally enforceable or customarily accepted; settled in cash, goods, services, shares…).

Debt vs equity

DebtEquity
RepaymentMandatoryNone
FlexibilityHigh (term, amount, refinancing)Low, high transaction costs, irreversible decision
CostInterest due whatever the income, market rateNo mandatory return; dividends if profits; higher expected return (risk)
TaxInterest usually deductibleDividends usually not deductible
PowerNo control over managementInfluence and control; dilution with new shareholders
Use of fundsCan be tied to a project (guarantees, mortgages)Not earmarked
Debt and equity play different risk/reward roles. Some companies have only private equity yet issue public debt (bonds). Analysts, shareholders and creditors all read this split.

Why year-end adjustments

Depreciation and impairment, accruals and deferrals, provisions, doubtful receivables: they apply the accruals, matching and prudence principles, cutting activity into annual periods at the closing date (often 31 December). The slides show a company can be very profitable with dangerously low cash (clients paying at two months, suppliers at one), or loss-making with rising cash.

Mechanism · Impairment of assets

Recoverable amount = max(fair value - costs of disposal; value in use) Impairment loss = carrying amount - recoverable amount (if positive)
  • Prudence: an asset may not sit on the books above its recoverable amount. Value in use = present value of the asset's expected cash flows.
  • One-off test, usually at closing. Reversal allowed if the recoverable amount rises again (IAS 36.114), capped at what the carrying amount would have been without impairment; never for goodwill.

Provisions

CauseTimingAmount
Certain liabilityReal and presentCertainCertain
Accrued expenseReal and presentNear certainUncertain
ProvisionReal and presentUncertainUncertain
Contingent liabilityPossible obligation, or present but unrecognizedUncertainUncertain
  • A provision is a liability of uncertain timing or amount. Three cumulative conditions: a present obligation (legal or constructive) from a past event; a probable outflow of resources; a reliable estimate. Otherwise no provision, only a contingent liability disclosed in the notes.
  • Accounting: an expense and a provision in liabilities, at the best estimate. Later: use (liability and cash both fall) or reversal (liability falls, revenue is recognized).

Class #6 · Statement of cash flows (13 Nov.)

Key concept · What the statement explains

The statement of cash flows explains the change in cash and cash equivalents (very liquid short-term investments with negligible risk of value change) over the period.

Operating cash flows (I) + Investing cash flows (II) = investment inflows - outflows + Financing cash flows (III) = financing inflows - outflows = Net change in cash (IV) Closing cash = opening cash + IV

The three activities

ActivityInflowsOutflows
OperatingSales of goods and services, royalties, commissionsPurchases, wages and social charges, taxes
InvestingDisposals of fixed assets, repayments of loans grantedPurchases of fixed assets, loans granted, securities (not cash equivalents)
FinancingShare issues, borrowingsShare buybacks, loan repayments
Interest and dividends. Until 2026 (IAS 7), a choice: interest and dividends received in operating or investing; paid in operating or financing; tax in operating. From 1 January 2027 (IAS 7 amended by IFRS 18), for most entities: received in investing, paid in financing, tax in operating. In the exam, read the classification instructions.

Mechanism · Direct and indirect methods

  • Direct: collections from customers minus payments to suppliers, employees, etc. (from actual cash movements).
  • Indirect: start from net income and correct it. A semi-direct variant corrects sales by the change in receivables, etc. Both methods give the same figure and concern only operating flows.
  • From 2027, the indirect method starts from operating profit.
Indirect method: Net income + depreciation, amortization and impairment charges, - reversals (non-cash items) - gains / + losses on disposals (remove disposal results) - increase in inventories and receivables (+ if decrease) + increase in trade and operating payables (- if decrease) = Operating cash flow

Class #7 · Introduction to Management Accounting; costing terms and purpose (20 Nov.)

Key concepts · What management accounting is

  • It measures and communicates financial and non-financial information to help managers decide (launch a product, accept a client, make or buy…) and shape strategy (cost leadership or differentiation).
  • Financial accounting: record, report outside, mandatory and standardized, annual, historical. Management accounting: specific to each organization, not mandatory, forward-looking, at any frequency (month, week, ad hoc). Management control uses this information to steer strategy and operations (budgets, variances, performance measurement).

Cost terms

  • Cost: a resource sacrificed to reach a goal. Cost object: anything whose cost we want to measure (brand, range, client, project, activity…).
  • Not all costs are expenses and vice versa: an investment is neither (cash down, asset up); depreciation is both a cost and an expense with no cash outflow.
DistinctionDefinitionKeep in mind
Variable / fixedVariable: varies in total with volume. Fixed: does not vary in total over the period despite volume.Depends on the contract and the horizon: the longer the horizon, the more costs are variable.
Direct / indirectDirect: traceable to the cost object in an economically feasible way. Indirect: linked to the object but not traceable; must be allocated.Depends on the cost object, the materiality of the cost, data collection technology, the organization.
Use unit costs cautiously. Unit cost = total cost / number of units. Kruger: fixed rent 94,500 + handlebar 52 per bike. At 1,000 bikes: (94,500 + 52,000)/1,000 = 146.50. At 600 bikes: (94,500 + 31,200)/600 = 209.50. Using 146.50 would understate the cost.

Mechanism · The cost-volume-profit (CVP) model

Profit = P x Q - v x Q - FC Contribution margin per unit = P - v Contribution margin ratio = (P - v) / P Breakeven volume = FC / (P - v) Breakeven revenue = FC / margin ratio Volume for a target profit = (FC + target profit) / (P - v) Margin of safety = sales - breakeven sales
  • Assumptions: volume is the only driver; costs split into fixed and variable, linear within the relevant range; price, unit costs and fixed costs known and constant; one product or a constant mix; no time value of money.
  • Uses: business plans, feasibility, profitability and risk diagnosis. Limits: single driver, linearity, constant mix, the fixed/variable split depends on the horizon.

Worked example · Dresses by Mary (official)

CVP and an advertising decision Class #7 slidesOfficial solution

Purchase 32 + other variable costs 10 per dress, price 70, fixed costs 84,000. Contribution per unit 28 (ratio 40%). At 2,500 dresses: 175,000 - 105,000 - 84,000 = -14,000. Breakeven: 84,000/28 = 3,000 dresses. An advertising campaign of 10,000 lifts sales from 3,200 to 4,000: profit goes from 5,600 to 18,000, i.e. +12,400 → run the campaign.

Relevant costs for decisions

  • Relevant costs and revenues: future costs and revenues that differ between options. Historical costs only help forecast; sunk costs are irrelevant.
  • Do not assume all variable costs are relevant, nor that all fixed costs are irrelevant. Full unit costs can mislead (irrelevant costs included; same unit cost at different volumes).
  • Opportunity cost: the contribution given up by not using a limited resource in its best alternative use; never recorded in accounting.
  • Scarce resource: at full capacity, rank products by contribution per unit of the scarce resource, not per unit of product.
  • Pricing: cost is only one input (competition, clients' ability to pay, perceived value); separate special sales from the regular price.
Noel (towels): capacity 44,000, production 30,000; variable 8.50 (6.50 + 0.50 + 1.50); fixed 150,000. Full cost (8.5×30,000 + 150,000)/30,000 = 13.50. A special order of 5,000 at 11.50: only variable costs change → contribution 3 × 5,000 = +15,000, accept (spare capacity exists).
Tiilikainen: motorbike engine, contribution 240 for 2h; boat engine, 375 for 5h; 600h available. Contribution per hour 120 vs 75 → favor motorbike engines.

Class #8 · Cost allocation: job order costing and process-costing (27 Nov.)

Why allocate indirect costs

  • Direct costs are traced; indirect costs are shared resources that must be allocated to build a full cost (pricing, portfolio strategy, cost reduction, full-cost inventory valuation).
Careful: never use a full cost to drop a product or outsource - reason with differential costs and revenues instead.

Key concepts

Full cost = traced direct costs + allocated indirect costs Cost per allocation unit = cost pool total / number of units of the allocation base Indirect cost charged = units consumed x cost per allocation unit
  • Cost pool: a grouping of indirect costs. Allocation base (cost driver, unite d'oeuvre): a measurable variable (hours, kg, euros, m2…) causally linked to the pool's costs. A homogeneous pool gathers costs with the same cause.
  • Choosing the driver: economic plausibility, quality of fit, regression slope.
  • Support pools (IT, HR, R&D, maintenance) vs operating pools (purchasing, production, distribution).

Job costing and process costing

ServicesManufacturing
Job costing (cost per order, batch or mission)Audit, consulting, ad campaignAircraft assembly, house building
Process costing (average cost of identical units)Deposit processing, standard mailRefining, food processing

Job-costing steps: identify the job; its direct costs; the relevant indirect pools; each pool's allocation base; the cost per allocation unit; then charge the job.

Mechanism · Allocating support pools

  1. Direct method: only services to operating pools count (simplest, most used).
  2. Step-down method: allocate first the support pool that serves the other support pools the most, then the next, with no return.
  3. Reciprocal method: all cross-services (equations); off syllabus. The French "centres d'analyse" method (PCG 1947) uses it.

Class #9 · Activity-Based Costing (4 Dec.)

Key concepts · Why ABC

  • Born in the US in the 1980s, when a single cost pool was no longer enough. Pools are multiplied to stay homogeneous and split by activities rather than by organizational departments.
  • No more support vs operating pools: every activity is charged to cost objects according to its consumption of drivers.

Mechanism · Implementing ABC

  1. Define the cost objects; (2) their direct costs; (3) the activities, their costs and their driver; compute the cost per driver; (4) charge according to driver consumption.
Cost per driver = activity cost / total number of drivers Cost charged to a product = Sum(drivers consumed x cost per driver)

Strengths and limits

  • Strengths: faithful modeling (especially of complexity: number of products, components), traceability, well suited to services and processes.
  • Limits: a heavy database (drivers x products) to build and maintain, risk of bureaucracy.
  • From ABC to ABM (activity-based management): cut costs, improve processes, plan activities, set prices and mix, think about customer value. About 40% of US companies use ABC, 20-35% in Europe and France.
Cutting the number of drivers of a product changes the split between products, not necessarily the company's total cost.
Class #10 · Introduction to budget and variance analysis (11 Dec.)

Key concepts · What a budget is

  • A quantified expression, over a limited period (usually one year), of a forward-looking view of the company, with financial and non-financial items. A reference point for action. Master budget and departmental budgets; no standard template; most are built on a projected income statement.
  • Approach: strategy → objectives → action plans → resources, from past performance and forecasts.
  • It sits in a wider process: strategic plan (3-5 years), capital budgets, operational plans (1-3 years), annual budget, departmental budgets (sales, production, materials, labor, overheads, cash, financing).

Common problems and control

  • Imposed without managers, a budget looks unrealistic and is little used; built with them, it takes time and triggers negotiations.
  • Control: compare budget and actual, adjust forecasts; this is the pivot of performance and variance analysis.

Mechanism · Variance analysis (sample exam "A la Coque")

Flexible budget = budget recomputed at the actual volume, with budgeted prices and unit costs Total (static budget) variance = actual - static budget Volume variance = flexible budget - static budget Flexible budget variance = actual - flexible budget A variance is favorable if it increases profit
The slides note that variance analysis was not covered in class, but it appears in a sample paper (A la Coque): know at least these three formulas.

Course wrap-up

Across Class #7-#10 you covered: the financial accounting / management accounting / control articulation; cost terms and their uses; decision-making with the CVP model; cost allocation methods (direct, step-down, ABC); and budgeting. Management accounting deals with information about the acquisition and consumption of resources, to make managers' decisions easier.

= Recoverable amount = max(fair value − costs of disposal; value in use)
= Impairment loss = carrying amount − recoverable amount
Provision: present obligation + probable outflow + reliable estimate; otherwise a contingent liability in the notes.
No provision for future losses; restructuring only once a formal plan is announced.
s6
= Change in cash = operating + investing + financing cash flows
Direct: receipts − payments; indirect: adjusted net income.
= Indirect: net income + depreciation − Δ receivables and inventory + Δ operating payables
Until 2026: choice for interest and dividends; from 2027: received → investing, paid → financing.
s7
Costs variable or fixed (by volume); direct or indirect (by cost object).
= Unit contribution margin = price − variable cost; margin rate = margin / price
= Break-even point = fixed costs / unit contribution margin
= Target volume = (fixed costs + target income) / unit contribution margin
Decide with relevant costs (future, differential); ignore sunk costs.
Scarce resource: margin per unit of the resource.
s8
= Cost per unit of work = cost centre cost / units of the allocation base
Job costing (by order) vs process costing (mass production).
Support centres: direct or sequential method.
Full cost is no basis for deciding to drop a product.
s9
ABC: indirect costs → activities → products via cost drivers.
= Cost per driver = activity cost / total drivers
Reveals the true cost of complex products (Alp'Ski, McCarthy, Stella Cuero).
Limit: heavy database; shifts costs between products.
Budget: a quantified expression of a forward-looking vision over a limited period.
= Flexible budget = budgeted unit prices and costs × actual volume
= Sales-volume variance = flexible budget − static budget
= Flexible-budget variance = actual − flexible budget
infos: Évaluation
Examen final le mardi 15 décembre 2026 au matin (DOME d'après MyESSEC), sur papier : 100 % de la note.
Financial accounting 60 %, management accounting 40 %.
Calculatrice 4 opérations seulement (pas de calculatrice financière à l'examen).
Rattrapage début 2027 ; échec au rattrapage = cours à refaire en 2027-2028.
Prérequis des cours CPTC 31125 et CPTG 31149.
Format de l'examen (sujets types Moodle)
Financial accounting : 12 QCM, puis des opérations aux états financiers (résultat 1 pt, bilan 2 pts, flux 3 pts).
Management accounting : exercices de calcul (coûts complets, centres, ABC, seuil, budget, écarts).
Les trois sujets types sont dans l'onglet Examen blanc, avec leurs corrigés.
Corrigés sur Moodle
Corrigés officiels publiés : Busoni, Schultz, Gerry Co., sujet type FA (exercice 2), sujets types MA 1 et 2.
Pas encore ouverts : Amorti, ACME et les cas de management accounting (Kuniyakino à Puyricard) ; la plateforme propose un corrigé selon la méthode du cours en attendant.
Le dossier « Sample examination » est encore vide ; un examen blanc est annoncé après la séance 10.
Méthode le jour J
Lire la consigne de classement des intérêts et dividendes avant le tableau des flux.
Pour chaque opération : effet sur actif, dettes, capitaux propres et trésorerie.
Vérifier que le bilan est équilibré.
Écrire la formule avant les chiffres : les points partiels comptent.
Arrondir seulement à la fin.
Supports et contacts
Slides FA 2026-2027 (S1-S6), slides MA (S7-S10), Workbook, Excel des cas, exercices additionnels, sujets types.
Lectures : Stolowy, Ding et Paugam (FA) ; Horngren (MA).
Exercices interactifs Moodle : quiz « The role of management accounting », « Speed Truck », Stereo Consulting et Vimeo (liens Quia).
Coordinateurs : Carlos Ramirez (FA), Adrian Zicari (MA).

qcm: [Class #1] Only events with a monetary impact (a potential effect on cash) are recorded in financial accounting. True or false?
False, every important event is recorded
False, only cash flows are recorded
Monetary unit convention: a decision or a hire with no measurable transaction is not recorded (Compofruit case).
[Class #1] Financial accounting is completely objective and leaves no room for judgment. True or false?
False, it involves decisions and subjectivity, hence rules and principles
The slides stress it: accounting is not mechanical.
[Class #1] Taking out a long-term bank loan affects:
Cash +X, loan (financial liability) +X; no effect on equity.
[Class #1] Which is usually NOT a current asset?
Equipment is used over several periods: a non-current asset.
A company buys equipment for 100 on credit. Effect on the accounting equation?
An asset comes in, a supplier liability appears; net income is untouched.
A company collects 42 from a customer receivable. Effect on total assets?
A simple reclassification within assets (Busoni, transaction 6).
Busoni sells on credit for 40 half of the goods bought for 60. Effect on net income?
Revenue 40, then cost of goods sold 60/2 = 30: net income +10.
Verdi repays 12 on its bank loan. Effect on net income?
Repaying principal reduces cash and the liability, not equity. Only interest is an expense.
Verdi: contribution of 150, loan of 60, equipment bought for 125 in cash. Total assets after these three transactions?
In the Verdi case, net income is 60 but operating cash flows are −1. Why?
70 of sales are not collected and part of the expenses are not paid: net income ≠ cash
Accrual principle: revenues and expenses do not coincide with receipts and payments.
Which measurement basis is easy to determine and verifiable, but does not track market value?
The advantage and limit of historical cost, per the slides.
From 2027, which standard replaces IAS 1 for the presentation of financial statements?
IFRS 18, adopted by the EU in February 2026, creates the operating profit and profit before financing and tax subtotals, among others.
[Class #2] Under IFRS 15, which is NOT a condition for recognising revenue from a sale of goods?
Control of the goods is transferred to the customer
The cash for the sale has been collected
The amount of consideration can be determined
Accounting is accrual-based: collection is not required.
[Class #2] When purchase costs rise, net income under FIFO is:
Lower than under LIFO or weighted average
Higher than under LIFO or weighted average
FIFO releases the oldest, cheapest inventory: lower cost of goods sold.
[Class #2] Why can year-end inventory be worth less than its carrying amount?
Inventory is measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
Uncollectible receivables must be written off
A receivable is uncollectible when the debtor is insolvent
Writing off an uncollectible receivable creates an expense
An impairment on a doubtful receivable can never be reversed
An impairment is reversed if the risk decreases.
Opening inventory 50 units at €100, purchase of 75 units at €110. Weighted average cost?
Cameras case: closing inventory value under FIFO?
The 25 units bought at 110 and the 25 at 120 remain: 2,750 + 3,000 = 5,750.
Mozart case: purchases of 200 units at €22 then 180 at €18; 260 units sold. Cost of goods sold under FIFO?
Mozart case (purchase prices falling: 22 then 18). Which method gives the highest net income?
Falling prices: LIFO releases the €18 units, the lowest cost of goods sold (5,000).
Purchase price 1,000, transport 60, customs duties 40, trade discount 50. Acquisition cost of the inventory?
1,000 + 60 + 40 − 50 = 1,050: discounts are deducted, transport and duties are added.
A receivable of 100 of which only 60 is expected to be collected. Effect on the year's net income?
None until the customer is liquidated
Impairment of 40 through an expense (Bruckner example, year X1).
Bruckner: accumulated impairment of 70 on a receivable of 100; the liquidated customer pays 10. Expense in the liquidation year?
Total loss 90, of which 70 already recognised: net expense 20.
A school collects in December X1 the tuition fees for the first term of X2. In X1 it must record:
Schultz exercise (a): the revenue belongs to X2.
Consignment sales: when does the consignor recognise revenue?
When the consignee sells the goods
Schultz exercise (d): unsold goods still belong to the consignor.
[Class #3] When an asset is sold mid-year, depreciation is recorded:
From the last depreciation charge (end of the previous period) to the disposal date
Pro rata temporis up to the disposal.
[Class #3] What happens when the carrying amount reaches the residual value?
The asset disappears from the balance sheet
The asset can stay in use, on the balance sheet at its residual value
Depreciation stops; the asset stays if it is still useful.
[Class #3] Amortising an intangible over the period it provides benefits applies the principle of:
The consumption of the asset is matched to the revenues it generates.
[Class #3] Brands can always be recognised as intangible assets. True or false?
True if it is well known
False: an internally generated brand is not recognised
Cost 11,000, residual value 1,000, 5 years, straight-line. Annual charge?
A 15,000 machine over 10 years, double declining balance. Year 2 charge?
Same machine (15,000, double declining over 10 years): carrying amount after 2 years?
Price 100, customs duties 5, transport 15, engineers' fees 30. Entry cost of the equipment?
All directly attributable costs to bring the asset to working condition are included.
Equipment with a carrying amount of 40 sold for 45. Effect on net income?
Gain on disposal = price − carrying amount = 5, presented net (IAS 16.68).
Land is not consumed: no depreciation.
Which can be recognised as an asset?
Only acquired goodwill (price − fair value of identifiable net assets) is recognised.
Amorti case: launch advertising of €100,000. Treatment?
Advertising is never an asset: immediate expense.
Amorti case: year 1 net income under straight-line (sales 1,000,000, other expenses 800,000, licence 15,000, advertising 100,000, line 60,000)?
Amorti case: over the 5 years, total net income under straight-line and declining balance is:
The method only changes the timing of the allocation.
ACME: share capital €5,000k, par value €25. Number of shares?
ACME raises €5,000k issuing shares at €100 (par value €25). Share premium?
ACME after the increase (equity €12,300k, 250,000 shares). Book value per share?
12,300,000 / 250,000 = €49.2: different from par value and market price.
Gerry Co.: opening reserves 50, net income 70, dividends declared 30. Reserves after appropriation?
Dividends declared but not yet paid appear:
They become an obligation to shareholders.
Which difference between liabilities and equity is correct?
Interest is due whatever the result
Interest is due even in a loss year, dividends are not.
Par value €10, 1,000 shares; issue of 160 shares at €25. Share capital after the issue?
[Class #5] Loan to an employee, annual interest of 120 due every 31 March. Interest revenue at 31 December?
Nine months accrued (April to December): 120 × 9/12 = 90, as accrued revenue.
Accrued interest not yet due is recorded at closing.
[Class #5] Annual rent of 1,200 paid in February N for 1 February N to 31 January N+1. Entry at end of N?
The month of January N+1 (100) was paid in advance.
[Class #5] Electricity billed on 31 January N for the last two months. No entry is needed at end of N−1. True or false?
True if the bill is small
False: an accrued expense must be recorded for December
When the warranted products are sold
At the end of the warranty
A provision is made at the time of sale to match the expense to the revenue.
It is not recognised, only disclosed in the notes
The conditions for a provision are not met.
[Class #5] A restructuring provision can be made as soon as management has decided to close an activity. True or false?
False: a formal plan and implementation started or an announcement are required
True if the amount is known
Case of the closure decided on 12 December without announcement: no provision.
Rent of 9,000 paid on 1 November N for November, December and January. Rent expense for year N?
Three months paid, two used in N: 6,000; 3,000 as a prepaid expense.
Annual subscription of 1,200 collected on 1 July N. Deferred revenue at 31 December N?
Six months remain to be served in N+1.
Invoice of 900 issued on 1 February N+1 for November, December and January. Accrued revenue at 31 December N?
Two of the three months belong to N.
10,000 warranted products: 75% no defect, 20% small defect (cost 1), 5% major defect (cost 10). Provision?
Carrying amount 1,200; fair value less costs of disposal 950; value in use 800. Impairment loss?
Imp case: carrying amount 600,000; value in use 800,000; net selling price 950,000. What to do?
Nothing: the recoverable amount exceeds the carrying amount
No impairment, and no upward revaluation under historical cost.
Can an impairment loss on goodwill be reversed?
Lawsuit: provision of 9M on the balance sheet, final settlement of 9.5M. Effect on the settlement year's net income?
The provision covers 9M; the additional expense is 0.5M.
Flossie Flowers: X2 loan interest (8,362) not recorded at 31/12/X2. Entry?
The X2 interest is incurred: accrued expense.
Offenbach: six-month insurance paid on 1 September X1. At 31 December X1:
January and February X2 were paid in advance.
Offenbach: one year's rent collected on 1 April X1 for a leased office. At 31 December X1:
Three months of rent belong to X2.
An airline must overhaul its planes every three years. A provision for future overhauls?
No: no present obligation arising from a past event
Yes, it is a legal obligation
Yes if the amount is reliable
Provisor case (d): the overhaul depends on future operations.
A lawsuit whose loss is probable and estimated at €350,000:
All three conditions for a provision are met (Provisor c).
[Class #6] Debt still owed at the end of year N never appears in N's cash flow statement. True or false?
True: the statement only shows flows
Balances are on the balance sheet; the statement only presents receipts and payments.
[Class #6] Under the direct method, which does NOT appear in operating cash flows?
Net income is the starting point of the indirect method.
[Class #6] Which is NOT a non-cash item?
Depreciation charge on tangible fixed assets
Paying tax is a real cash outflow.
Each one is a cash inflow.
Net income 100; depreciation 50; trade receivables +30; trade payables +20. Operating cash flows (indirect method)?
The purchase of a machine paid in cash is reported in:
From 2027 (IAS 7 amended by IFRS 18), where does interest paid go for most companies?
Interest and dividends received in investing, paid in financing.
Beethoven case: operating cash flows of X2?
Beethoven case: net income of X2?
A capital increase of 240 paid in cash is reported in:
Price £70, variable cost £42, fixed costs £84,000. Break-even point?
Montvert: price €2, variable cost €1.20, fixed costs €3.6M, 10M units. Net income?
Montvert: variable cost rises by €0.16. New break-even point?
Walk-About: price £30, variable cost £21, fixed costs £360,000. Net income at 35,000 pairs?
Walk-About: indifference volume between the commission plan (margin 9, fixed 360,000) and the fixed plan (margin 10.50, fixed 441,000)?
Speed Truck: price €1,200, variable cost €250, fixed costs €104,000. Trucks for a profit of €57,500?
Noel: variable cost €8.50, full cost €13.50, spare capacity. Special order of 5,000 towels at €11.50?
Tiilikainen at full capacity: motorbike engine (margin €240, 2 h) and boat engine (€375, 5 h). Which engine to favour?
With a scarce resource, rank by margin per unit of resource.
Kruger: fixed €94,500, variable €52 per bike. Unit cost for 600 bikes?
(94,500 + 31,200) / 600: the €146.50 unit cost computed at 1,000 bikes would understate it.
Which cost is NOT relevant for a decision?
A future cost that differs between options
Sunk costs do not change with the decision.
My new car: differential cost per business kilometre?
€4,290 of extra costs for 15,000 km; the €0.35 offer is acceptable.
Kuniyakino: the sales commission of the Management department head is:
Specific to the department and linked to sales.
Kuniyakino: the store's single electricity bill is, for the Management department:
It covers the whole store and does not depend on sales.
Immoservices: £21,000 of indirect costs, 200 hours. Rate per hour?
Immoservices (single cost centre): cost of the Pemberley engagement (104 h at £70 + indirect costs)?
Immoservices with two centres (administration £35/h, documentation £1,400 per request; Pemberley 2 requests). Cost of Pemberley?
Slides example, direct method: maintenance 600,000 allocated on the main centres' hours (machining 2,400 h, assembly 4,000 h). Machining's share?
Same example, sequential method: maintenance allocated first (20% to IT). IT cost to be allocated next?
WattWatt: overhead 2,400,000, direct labour 1,500,000. Overhead charged to contract Alpha (labour 300,000)?
Which industry is typical of process costing?
Alp'Ski: total of the Cutting centre after allocating support centres?
Should a product's full cost be used to decide to drop that product?
No: a differential cost and revenue analysis is needed
Yes if the product is loss-making
Allocated indirect costs often remain after dropping it (cf. Puyricard, option A).
McCarthy: cutting 231,000 €; 3,600 h (mass retail) and 250 h (institutional catering). Cost per cutting hour?
McCarthy under ABC: cost of a kg of fries for institutional catering?
Stella Cuero: machine setups €24,250 for 2,500 setups. Cost per setup?
Stella Cuero: Toledo's result under ABC (sales 240,000, direct 218,400, ABC indirect 15,690)?
240,000 − 218,400 − 15,690; under the cost-centre method, Toledo lost 3,000.
Alp'Ski under ABC: which ski becomes loss-making?
GRIMPER (small batches, many setups and drying): −7,824.
What is a limit of ABC?
A heavy database to build and maintain
It distorts the cost of complex products
Number of drivers × number of products.
Under ABC, reducing the number of drivers a product consumes:
Always reduces the company's total cost
A la Coque: flexible-budget operating income (15,000 units, price €40, variable €4.50, fixed 42,000)?
A la Coque: sales-volume variance on operating income?
A la Coque: flexible-budget variance on operating income?
Castelo Branco: 2025 revenue (k€) with equipment 6,000 × 1.10 × 1.06 and contracts 1,800 × 1.06?
Smell Good: volume sold with 20,000 samples (150 sales per 100) and the media campaign (+15,000), base 10,000?
Smell Good: launch result (55,000 units at €250, 5% discount, cost €90, samples €20,000, media €300,000)?
Puyricard, option A (dropping the marrons glacés: net margin of 295,000 lost, 84,000 of savings):
The indirect costs allocated to the marrons mostly remain.
Cityline: the Dualtron product manager proposes €500 for 16,000 units. Overall result:
Dualtron's direct-cost margin falls by 100,000; overheads are only redistributed.
Which statement about the budget is correct?
It is the quantified expression of a forward-looking vision over a limited period

[Sample paper FA, Q1] Cash-collected sales 2,000; purchases paid 1,000; depreciation 100; interest 50; receivables decrease 30; trade payables increase 60; non-operating interest. Operating cash flows?
2,000 − 1,000 + 30 + 60; depreciation is not a flow and interest is excluded.
[Sample paper FA, Q2] An increase in trade payables has what effect on cash?
[Sample paper FA, Q3] Which is NOT an accounting principle or convention?
[Sample paper FA, Q4] Which is recognised as an asset?
Only the patent is an identifiable asset.
[Sample paper FA, Q5] Equity at end of 2015: 19,200 (including net income 1,200). In 2016: net income 600, dividends 500, land contribution of 800. Equity and net income at end of 2016?
[Sample paper FA, Q6] Equipment of 1,200; depreciation 150 then 175; impairment of 50. Carrying amount at end of 2016?
[Sample paper FA, Q7] 1,000 shares of €10 par value; contribution of a building worth €3,000 and €1,000 against shares issued at €25. Which statement is false?
[Sample paper FA, Q8] Which situation cannot give rise to a provision?
A lawsuit brought by a customer
Timing and amount are almost certain: it is not a provision.
[Sample paper FA, Q9] Goods purchased for 2,000; half resold for 1,800; next year's rent paid 300. Net income?
1,800 − 1,000; the prepaid rent is not an expense of the year.
[Sample paper FA, Q10] A car dealer's purchase of cars belongs to which cycle?
For the dealer, cars are inventory.
[Sample paper FA, Q11] A €10,000 machine, 5 years, estimated resale €1,000. Straight-line depreciation in year 1?
[Sample paper FA, Q12] Same machine under double declining balance: year 1 charge?
40% × 10,000 (residual value is not deducted under declining balance).

Cityline, single allocation base: Dualtron's result?

Sujet type fourni sur Moodle (« Final Quiz FA sample »). Format de la partie FA de l'examen : 12 QCM, puis un exercice des opérations aux états financiers (compte de résultat 1 point, bilan 2 points, flux de trésorerie 3 points). Les 12 QCM sont aussi dans l'onglet QCM.

E1 · 12 QCM Moodle · Final Quiz FA sampleCorrigé proposé
  1. Alpha, 2018 : ventes encaissées 2 000 ; achats payés 1 000 ; amortissement 100 ; intérêts 50 ; baisse des créances clients 30 ; hausse des dettes fournisseurs 60. Les intérêts payés ne sont pas des flux opérationnels. Flux opérationnels ? a) 1 240 b) 1 090 c) 1 010 d) 1 060
  2. Effet d'une hausse des dettes fournisseurs sur la trésorerie ? a) négatif b) aucun c) positif d) négatif ou positif
  3. Lequel n'est pas un principe comptable ? a) rattachement (matching) b) « incurring » c) engagement (accruals) d) prudence
  4. Lequel est comptabilisé à l'actif ? a) goodwill créé en interne b) dépenses de recherche c) publicité qui devrait tripler les ventes d) un brevet
  5. Distribute SA fin 2015 : capital 10 000, prime 5 000, réserves 3 000, résultat 1 200. En 2016 : résultat 600, dividendes 500, apport d'un terrain de 800. Capitaux propres et résultat fin 2016 ? a) 20 100 et 600 b) 20 100 et 100 c) 19 300 et 600 d) 19 300 et 1 400
  6. Équipement acheté début 2015 : 1 000 comptant + 200 à payer. Amortissement 150 en 2015, 175 en 2016, dépréciation de 50 en 2016. Valeur comptable fin 2016 ? a) 625 b) 875 c) 825 d) 775
  7. Share Co. : 1 000 actions de nominal 10 €. Elle reçoit un immeuble de 3 000 € et 1 000 € en espèces contre des actions émises à 25 €. Quelle affirmation est fausse ? a) les capitaux propres augmentent de 4 000 b) le capital est de 10 000 c) la prime augmente de 2 400 d) 160 actions sont émises
  8. Quelle situation ne peut pas donner lieu à une provision ? a) une restructuration b) une vente avec garantie c) un procès d'un client d) une charge à payer
  9. Achat de marchandises 2 000 (moitié payée) ; vente de la moitié pour 1 800 (moitié encaissée) ; loyer de l'an prochain payé 300. Résultat ? a) 500 b) 100 c) 800 d) 300
  10. L'achat de voitures par un concessionnaire relève du cycle : a) d'investissement b) d'exploitation c) de financement d) exceptionnel
  11. Beta : machine de 10 000 € début 2016, 5 ans, valeur de revente 1 000. Amortissement linéaire de la 1ʳᵉ année ? a) 2 000 b) 1 800 c) 2 200 d) aucune
  12. Même machine, dégressif double : 1ʳᵉ année ? a) 4 000 b) 3 600 c) 3 000 d) 2 000

Le corrigé officiel n'est pas encore publié sur Moodle : ce corrigé applique la méthode du cours, étape par étape.

1b) 1 090On traite 2 000 et 1 000 comme ventes et achats de l'exercice : 2 000 − 1 000 + 30 (baisse des créances) + 60 (hausse des dettes) ; l'amortissement n'est pas un flux, les intérêts sont exclus.
2c) positifLes achats non payés conservent de la trésorerie.
3b) incurringCe n'est pas un principe comptable.
4d) un brevetActif incorporel identifiable ; les trois autres ne sont jamais des actifs.
5a) 20 100 et 60019 200 + 600 − 500 + 800 = 20 100 ; le résultat 2016 est 600.
6c) 8251 200 − 150 − 175 − 50.
7b) est fausse4 000/25 = 160 actions : capital +1 600 → 11 600 ; prime +160 × 15 = 2 400.
8d) une charge à payerMontant et échéance quasi certains : ce n'est pas une provision.
9c) 800Ventes 1 800 − coût des ventes 1 000 ; le loyer payé d'avance est une charge constatée d'avance.
10b) exploitationLes voitures sont le stock du concessionnaire.

12a) 4 000Taux 2 × 20 % = 40 % appliqué au coût de 10 000.

Trottinettes électriques Thunder (10 000 unités, 700 €) et Dualtron (20 000 unités, 450 €). Schultz exercise (revenue recognition) Moodle · Additional exercise SchultzOfficial solution

(a) A school invoices on 1 December X1 the fees for the first term of X2, all collected on 15/12, and recognizes revenue on collection. (b) A shipyard builds a cargo ship (started July X2, 10% complete at end X2, 80% at end X3, delivered April X4; estimated cost 80M) and recognizes revenue on delivery. (c) A bridge club spreads membership fees linearly over the membership period. (d) A shipper entrusts goods to a consignee who sells them on its behalf, and recognizes revenue on delivery to the consignee.

See the solution
  • (a) Wrong: the revenue belongs to X2 (deferred revenue), even if the cash is collected in X1.
  • (b) Revenue should rather be recognized over time (percentage of completion), since revenue, costs and progress are reliably measurable.
  • (c) Correct.
  • (d) Wrong: revenue is recognized when the consignee sells the goods; unsold goods return to the shipper.

Schultz exercise (revenue recognition) Moodle · Additional exercise SchultzOfficial solution

(a) A school invoices on 1 December X1 the fees for the first term of X2, all collected on 15/12, and recognizes revenue on collection. (b) A shipyard builds a cargo ship (started July X2, 10% complete at end X2, 80% at end X3, delivered April X4; estimated cost 80M) and recognizes revenue on delivery. (c) A bridge club spreads membership fees linearly over the membership period. (d) A shipper entrusts goods to a consignee who sells them on its behalf, and recognizes revenue on delivery to the consignee.

See the solution
  • (a) Wrong: the revenue belongs to X2 (deferred revenue), even if the cash is collected in X1.
  • (b) Revenue should rather be recognized over time (percentage of completion), since revenue, costs and progress are reliably measurable.
  • (c) Correct.
  • (d) Wrong: revenue is recognized when the consignee sells the goods; unsold goods return to the shipper.
