Case Flossie Flowers (Workbook) WorkbookProposed solution

Entries at 31/12/X2. (A) Flowers delivered on 27/12/X2, the 2,400 invoice sent on 05/01/X3. (B) Internet access bill of 01/12/X2 covering December and January, 200, paid on 15/12. (C) Estimated December expenses: phone 480 (administration), electricity and heating 620 (distribution), bills arriving in January. (D) Loan of 100,000 from 01/01/X1 at 10%, repaid in constant annual instalments of 26,380 each January; nothing recorded for X2, of which principal 18,018 and interest 8,362.

See the solution

The official solution is not published on Moodle yet: this one applies the course method, step by step.

AssetsLiabilitiesEquity (income)
AAccrued revenue (unbilled) +2,400Sales +2,400
BPrepaid expense +100 (January)Internet expense -100 (the X2 expense is only 100)
CAccrued expenses +1,100Phone -480; electricity and heating -620
DAccrued interest +8,362; 18,018 of the loan reclassified as currentInterest expense -8,362

Check D: X1 interest = 10% × 100,000 = 10,000, principal repaid 16,380, balance 83,620; X2 interest = 8,362, principal 18,018 (total 26,380).

Case Imp (Workbook) WorkbookProposed solution

Machine bought on 02/01/20X3 for 3,000,000, depreciated straight-line over 5 years (600,000 per year). Impairment test at end 20X6: useful life unchanged, value in use 800,000, net selling price 950,000. Accounting effects in 20X6?

See the solution

The official solution is not published on Moodle yet: this one applies the course method, step by step.

After the 20X6 charge (4th year), net book value = 3,000,000 - 4 × 600,000 = 600,000. Recoverable amount = max(950,000; 800,000) = 950,000. It exceeds the carrying amount: no impairment loss. Only the normal 600,000 charge is recorded, and the asset is not revalued upwards.

If the test were done before the 20X6 charge (NBV 1,200,000), the loss would be 1,200,000 - 950,000 = 250,000. Always check the date of the test.

Case Provisor (Workbook) WorkbookProposed solution

Provision or not? (a) One-year warranty, 3,000,000 of sales, 1-3% of products defective and replaced. (b) Phosphate extraction on own land, estimated restoration costs 5,000,000. (c) Lawsuit, loss judged probable, 350,000. (d) Airline legally required to overhaul its planes every three years, future cost estimated at 2,500,000.

See the solution

The official solution is not published on Moodle yet: this one applies the course method, step by step.

  • (a) Yes: present obligation (past sales), probable outflow, estimable: between 30,000 and 90,000, e.g. 60,000 (2%) from experience.
  • (b) Yes only if a legal or constructive obligation to restore exists (law, public commitment). Otherwise no provision (like the slide's oil company while no law exists).
  • (c) Yes: provision of 350,000.
  • (d) No: the overhaul relates to future operation of the planes, not a past event; the company could sell the planes. No present obligation, so no provision (and future operating losses or expenses are never provided for).

Kuniyakino (cost terms) Official Kuniyakino solution opens on Moodle 21 Nov, 12:00Proposed solution

A Singapore bookshop, Management department. Classify each cost as direct or indirect (relative to the department) and variable or fixed (relative to the number of books sold): 1. shop electricity (single bill); 2. books bought for resale; 3. subscription to the magazine Business Books for leaders; 4. accounting software rental; 5. store manager's salary; 6. commission on the department head's sales; 7. free bookmarks (one per customer); 8. metro advertising; 9. fire insurance; 10. merchandising for the launch of Innovative Strategies.

See the solution

The official solution is not published on Moodle yet: this one applies the course method, step by step.

CostD / IV / F
1 ElectricityIF
2 Books boughtDV
3 Magazine subscriptionDF
4 Accounting softwareIF
5 Store managerIF
6 Department head's commissionDV
7 BookmarksIV
8 Metro advertisingIF
9 Fire insuranceIF
10 Book merchandisingDF

The bookmark is given to all shop customers (indirect for the department) but its cost follows the number of customers (variable).

Montvert (breakeven) Official Montvert solution opens on Moodle 21 Nov, 19:00Proposed solution

Pens sold at 2; 2024 sales: 20M euros; fixed costs 3,600,000; variable cost 1.20. (1) Current profit and breakeven in volume and revenue. (2) Independent questions: (a) variable cost +0.16; (b) advertising +360,000 of fixed costs and +10% volume; (c) 20% discount, volume +40%, variable cost -10%; (d) move upmarket: price +10%, fixed costs +80,000.

See the solution

The official solution is not published on Moodle yet: this one applies the course method, step by step.

Volume 20M / 2 = 10M units. Unit margin 2 - 1.20 = 0.80.

CaseUnit marginVolumeFixedProfitBreakeven (units)Breakeven (revenue)
Current0.8010M3.6M4.4M4.5M9M
(a)0.6410M3.6M2.8M5.625M11.25M
(b)0.8011M3.96M4.84M4.95M9.9M
(c) price 1.60, v 1.080.5214M3.6M3.68M≈ 6.92M≈ 11.08M
(d) price 2.201.0010M (unchanged)3.68M6.32M3.68M8.10M

Moving upmarket (d) maximizes profit if volume holds; the promotion (c) raises the breakeven sharply.

Walk-About (CVP) Official Walk-About solution opens on Moodle 21 Nov, 19:00Proposed solution

Shoe shop: price 30 per pair, 5% commission, shoe cost 19.50; fixed: rent 60,000, salaries 200,000, advertising 80,000, other 20,000. (1) Breakeven in units and revenue; profit at 35,000 pairs. (2) If the manager gets 0.30 per pair. (3) Commission removed against +81,000 of fixed salaries: (a) breakeven; (b) indifference volume between the two plans; (c) profits at 50,000 and 60,000 pairs; (d) volume for a target profit of 168,000.

See the solution

The official solution is not published on Moodle yet: this one applies the course method, step by step.

Variable cost 19.50 + 1.50 = 21; margin 9; fixed 360,000.

  1. Breakeven 360,000/9 = 40,000 pairs, i.e. 1,200,000. At 35,000: 35,000 × 9 - 360,000 = -45,000.
  2. Margin 8.70 → breakeven 41,379.3, rounded to 41,380 pairs (1,241,400).
  3. (a) Margin 10.50, fixed 441,000 → breakeven 42,000 pairs (1,260,000). (b) 10.5Q - 441,000 = 9Q - 360,000 → Q = 54,000. (c) 50,000 pairs: fixed 84,000, commission 90,000; 60,000 pairs: fixed 189,000, commission 180,000. Beyond 54,000, the fixed plan pays more. (d) Fixed: (441,000 + 168,000)/10.5 = 58,000; commission: (360,000 + 168,000)/9 = 58,667 pairs.
My new car (relevant costs) Official My new car solution opens on Moodle 28 Nov, 19:00Proposed solution

New car for 19,750, 25,000 km a year of personal use. The employer offers 0.35/km for 15,000 business km a year. The car is changed around 75,000 to 80,000 km (trade-in at market). Resale values: 15,200 (1 yr), 14,350 (2 yrs), 13,450 (3 yrs), 12,100 (4 yrs), 10,200 (5 yrs). Insurance 600/yr (private) or 900/yr (private + business); parking 600/yr; 9 l/100 km at 1.40/l; maintenance 0.10/km. Accept?

See the solution

The official solution is not published on Moodle yet: this one applies the course method, step by step.

Annual costWithout business (25,000 km)With business (40,000 km)
Value lossResale after 3 yrs (75,000 km): 6,300/3 = 2,100Resale after 2 yrs (80,000 km): 5,400/2 = 2,700
Insurance600900
Parking600600
Fuel (0.126/km)3,1505,040
Maintenance2,5004,000
Total8,95013,240

Differential cost: 4,290 for 15,000 km, i.e. 0.286/km < 0.35: accept (a gain of about 960 a year). Parking is not relevant (identical in both cases); the purchase price is already paid, only the resale value difference matters.

Immoservices (job costing) Official Immoservices solution not open on Moodle yetProposed solution

Real-estate consulting firm, price = cost + 30%. Direct labor: 70/h; a single indirect pool (21,000) allocated per hour. Pemberley: 104 h; Netherfield: 96 h. (2) Cost and price of each engagement. McCarthy (ABC) Official McCarthy solution not open on Moodle yetProposed solution

Frozen fries: 1,000,000 kg (900,000 retail, 100,000 catering). Potatoes 150,000; production support 983,000 allocated per kg. (1) Cost per kg. (2) 188,000 of packaging becomes direct (180,000 retail, 8,000 catering), the rest per kg. (3) Activities: washing 120,000 (kg); cutting 231,000 (hours: 250 kg/h retail, 400 kg/h catering); packing 444,000 (hours: 25 kg/h retail, 100 kg/h catering). Cost per driver, cost per kg per market, use of the information.

See the solution

The official solution is not published on Moodle yet: this one applies the course method, step by step.

  1. (150,000 + 983,000)/1,000,000 = 1.133/kg for everyone.
  2. Remaining 795,000/1,000,000 = 0.795/kg. Retail: 0.15 + 0.795 + 180,000/900,000 (0.20) = 1.145; catering: 0.15 + 0.795 + 0.08 = 1.025.
  3. Washing 0.12/kg. Cutting: 3,600 h retail + 250 h catering = 3,850 h → 60/h. Packing: 36,000 h + 1,000 h = 37,000 h → 12/h.
Cost per kgRetailCatering
Potatoes0.150.15
Direct packaging0.200.08
Washing0.120.12
Cutting216,000/900,000 = 0.2415,000/100,000 = 0.15
Packing432,000/900,000 = 0.4812,000/100,000 = 0.12
Total1.190.62

The catering market costs 0.62/kg, not 1.133: the old system overcharged it, hence a bid priced 30% too high. Uses: pricing tenders, market profitability analysis, reducing activity costs (ABM).

ACCOUNTING

MANAGEMENT CONTROL

DEPARTMENT

Year 2026/2027

Pre-Msc Accounting CPTC 31081

Financial Accounting

CASES

Verdi

(Adapted from Stolowy, Lebas and Ding, 2011)

Stefania, a professional photographer, and her life partner Stefano, a graphic-design artist, decide to create an advertising agency on 1 January X1.

Transaction # 1

The financial resources they wish to invest in their business venture amount to CU150. They create their business (company) with a capital contribution of CU150.

They agree that Stefania receive 100 shares with a nominal par value of CU1 (as she contributed two-thirds of the initial capital), while Stefano receive 50 shares. They choose to name their business venture ‘Verdi’ and open a bank account in that name. Each shareholder deposits the agreed upon amount of cash in the bank account.

Transaction # 2

Early in January X1, Verdi obtains a CU60 loan from its bank. The principal of the loan is deposited in Verdi’s bank account. The contract specifies that the interest shall be paid at the end of each period, on the remaining principal.

Transaction # 3

Early January X1 Verdi acquires some equipment (a computer, a color printer, and an art/drawing software program). These cost CU125 in total. The supplier is paid for this purchase with a check drawn on Verdi’s bank account.

Transaction # 4

Sam Suffit, a retailer, approaches Verdi on 14 January and contracts for an advertising campaign to be carried out in February for his spring season products. After agreeing on the content and format of the campaign, Sam Suffit agrees to pay CU250 for the service Verdi will render, 30 days after he receives the invoice, which will be sent after the advertising campaign has been implemented.

Transaction # 5

On 31 March Sam Suffit sends a check for CU180 of the CU250 debt to Verdi; this check is immediately deposited in Verdi’s bank account.

Transaction # 6a

In order to carry out the advertising campaign referred to in Transaction 4, Verdi paid wages to employees in the amount of CU101, including social contributions and benefits. This payment will be carried out by writing a check. For simplicity, we will assume here that the wage cost plus social contributions and benefits are paid in one single operation.

Transaction # 6b

The lending institution withdraws at the end of the period the interest accrued, which amounts to CU4.

Transaction # 6c

Verdi has received an invoice from a supplier (a subcontracted special effects artist) who worked on specific aspects of the Sam Suffit campaign. The invoice is in the amount of CU85 and is due within 60 days of receipt.

Transaction # 7

Verdi only settles CU80 out of the CU85 supplier’s claim (accounts payable) on the due date. The remaining CU5 will be settled at a later date.

Transaction # 8

Verdi partially reimburses the lender by returning CU12 on the loan it contracted above.

Required:

Determine the impact of these transactions on the business equation.

Prepare Verdi’s main financial statements at the end of X1.

Busoni

Busoni is set up as a business on Sept 30, 20X1.

The shareholders bring equipment (CU100) and cash (CU40) as contribution to the company’s capital on Sept. 30

Merchandise is purchased on credit, on Oct 4, for CU60

A bank loan is granted to the company, on Oct. 5, for CU100

The company renders services on Oct. 5, on credit, for CU50

Personnel expenses are paid by the company on Oct. 15, for CU20

Cash is received from customers on prior sales, on Oct. 17, for CU42

Half the merchandise purchased in 2) is sold, on credit, for a selling price of CU40, on Oct. 18

An invoice is received from providers of utilities, for the current consumption, for CU15, on Oct. 19

Merchandise suppliers are partly paid, for CU45, on Oct. 20

The company repays to the bank CU10 on its loan, on Oct. 22.

1) What is the impact of each transaction on the business equation?

2) Prepare a Statement of profit or loss (an Income Statement) and a Statement of Financial Position (a Balance Sheet) for Busoni, based on these transactions only

3. Mozart

(case prepared by Thomas Jeanjean; updated by Catalin Albu)

Mozart Company, a retailer selling a single product, opened shop on 1 April. April’s transactions were as follows:

April 01: Capital contribution of CU5000 was received from the shareholders.

April 02: Purchase of 200 units @ CU22 each, paid in cash.

April 08: Purchase of 180 units @ CU18 each, on credit (due at the end of May).

April 17: Sale of 240 units @ CU25 each, for cash.

April 22: Payment of rent for CU500 for April.

April 25: Sale of 20 units @ CU26 each, on credit (to be collected in May).

April 27: Payment of salaries for CU400 for April.

April 30: Payment of income taxes, related to all transactions between April 1 and 29.

The income tax rate is 40%.

Required:

Using successively each of the three costing methods (FIFO, LIFO, and WAC), prepare Mozart’s main financial statements (Statement of financial position (Balance sheet), Statement of profit or loss (income statement), statement of cash flows) at the end of April.

prepare a table allowing to compare the impact of the three methods on:

the ending inventory;

the net income;

the cash flow

4. Amorti

A company is considering investing in a project with a five-year useful life. The project involves paying €75 000 for a licence to manufacture a new product and equipping a production line at a cost of €300 000. In order to launch the product the company plans a three-month advertising campaign which will cost €100 000.

Assuming that in each year the expected sales are €1 000 000 and expenses other than those detailed above are €800 000, draw up two alternative series of income statements for the project in the first two years of use, by using (a) the straight-line method, and (b) the diminishing balance method at 40 per cent per annum, for the production line. In both sets, decide whether the licence and the advertising campaign should be recognized as assets or as expenses, and treat them identically in the two sets.

5. ACME

(case prepared by: Thomas Jeanjean; updated by Catalin Albu)

ACME group is a public limited company. The firm was created 5 years ago with a capital contribution from its shareholders of 5000 k€. The par value of each share is €25. Since then, ACME has been relatively profitable and distributed generous dividends while increasing the level of retained earnings.

The firm needs 5000k€ of additional cash to fund its development projects. The general assembly agrees to lever this sum through a capital increase. The market price of ACME shares is 110€ per share. Shareholders agreed to sell new shares at €100.

You will find in the appendix an excerpt from the ACME balance sheet (Equity section of the balance sheet).

Required:

Compute the number of shares at the creation of ACME.

Compute the number of shares that ACME needs to issue to lever the 5000k€ required.

Discuss the impact of the capital increase on the balance sheet and present the equity section of ACME after the capital increase.

Appendix: Equity section of the balance sheet (in k€)

Share capital5,000
Retained earnings1,500
Net income800

Flossie Flowers is a florist company. Please help its accountant record the following operations for the year X2

A) On 27 December X2, Flossie Flowers has delivered a set of floral arrangements to one of its clients. The client is billed €2 400 but the invoice is to be sent to him only on 5 January X3. Make the relevant entries for December X2 regarding this transaction.

AssetsAssets=LiabilitiesLiabilities+Shareholders’ equityShareholders’ equity
Heading

C) Flossie Flowers estimates expenses for December of €480 for telephone (administration) and €620 for light and heat (distribution). The invoices will be issued in January X3. Make the relevant entries regarding this transaction on 31 December X2.

Although the annuity for the year X1 has been correctly recorded and paid, nothing has been done for the year X2. Make the relevant entries regarding this transaction on 31 December X2. For the year X2, figures are as follows: repayment of loan = €18 018 and interest = €8 362.

7. Imp

On 2 January, 20X3 a company purchased a specialized machine tool for £3 000 000. The straight-line depreciation schedule established an annual depreciation charge of £600 000 over a five-year useful life. Changes in market demand brought the company to carry out an impairment test at the end of accounting period 20X6.

The impairment test was executed by external valuation experts and they concluded that (a) the original useful life was still appropriate, (b) the net present value calculation of the cash flows to be generated by the machine tool amounted to £800 000 and (c) £950 000 is a reasonable estimate of the net selling price of the machine tool at the time of the impairment test.

What are the accounting effects of this impairment test for accounting period 20X6?

8. Provisor

Critically assess whether a provision should be set up in each of the following cases:

(a) Company A offers a one-year warranty for the products that it manufactures. Yearly revenue subject to product warranties amounts to €3 000 000. In past years between 1 per cent and 3 per cent of the products proved defective. Defective products are replaced.

(b) Company B produces and sells phosphate fertilizers that are used to grow grains. The process of extracting the raw materials from the land the company owns, has a major impact on the natural environment. At balance sheet date, estimates of environmental remediation costs amount to €5 000 000.

(c) A lawsuit claiming damages has been filed against company C. The company’s legal advisers consider the loss probable and have estimated potential settlement costs at €350 000.

(d) Company D runs an airline. The company is required by law to overhaul its aircraft once every three years. The future maintenance costs are estimated at €2 500 000.

9. Beethoven Company

(adapted from Stolowy, Lebas and Ding, 2011)

The balance sheet prepared by the Beethoven Co. at 31 December X1 is presented below:

Balance sheet at 31 December X1 (in 000 €)

Non-current assets900Shareholders’ equity1,010
Manufacturing equipment900Share capital 400
Retained earnings250
Net income of X1360
Current assets560Liabilities450
Inventories 200Bank loans120
Accounts receivable220Accounts payable90
Cash at bank140Income tax payable240
Total assets1,460Total E&L1,460

The following transactions happened during X2 (all in 000 €):

1. it sold merchandise for 1,600 (of which 1,400 collected during the year).

2. it purchased merchandise for 500 (of which 480 paid during the year).

3. it repaid 50 on the bank loan; it contracted another bank loan for 70; it paid interest expense of 45 for the year.

4. it paid salaries and social contributions of 450.

5. it paid rent for 300.

6. it paid other expenses for 75.

7. it purchased new manufacturing equipment for 200 (entirely paid during the year).

8. it recorded depreciation of the manufacturing equipment of 50 for the entire year.

9. New capital is issued and paid in cash: 240 (entirely received during the year, shares issued at par).

10. Ending inventories: 220

The income tax rate is 40%. The income tax expense on X2 income will be paid in X3.

Required:

Prepare the statement of cash flows, the income statement and the balance sheet at the end of X2

Full text of the original handout (English)
Pre-Msc Accounting CPTC 31081




           Schultz
            Solution



                                1


  Schultz

  (a) DPS Business School Inc. (DPSBS Inc.) invoices its students at the beginning
  of each quarter for the quarterly tuition fees. DPSBS Inc. recognizes revenue only
  when tuition is actually paid by the students (or whomever, on their behalf). The
  first quarter X2 tuition invoices were mailed on 1 December X1 and all the tuition
  fee payments have been received in full by 15 December X1. No adjusting entry
  has been recorded.

  Revenues should be recognized when earned and not when cash is received.
  Even if the tuition fees have been paid in X1 (cash increase), the revenue belongs
  to the year X2 (Prepaid or Deferred revenue)




ESSEC                                                                                  2


  Schultz

  (b) Merseyside Ship-building receives an order to build a cargo ship. The work starts on July
  1 20X2. At 31 December 20X2 the ship is 10% complete, and at the end of next year is 80%
  complete. The ship leaves the yard in April 20X4. During this period Merseyside Ship-building
  received the following payments: 20 Million EUR in 20X2, 60 Million EUR in 20X3 and 20
  Million in 20X4. The estimated cost of the ship is 80 Million EUR. Revenue is recognized
  upon completion and delivery of the ship.

  Completed-contract vs percentage of completion method

  Here it should be rather the percentage of completion method (revenue, related costs and
  progress can be measured reliably)




ESSEC                                                                                             3


  Schultz

  (c) A bridge club invoices a membership fee to its members who receive in return
  the magazine ‘Bridge Forever’ and are entitled to specially discounted prices on
  other magazines produced by the same publisher. The club, in order to simplify its
  recording of fees, spreads the fee revenue on a straight-line basis over the period
  of membership.

  OK




ESSEC                                                                                   4


  Schultz

  (d) A seller (shipper) transfers goods to a buyer (recipient) who undertakes to sell
  the goods on behalf of the seller (consignment sales). The shipper recognizes the
  revenue at the time of delivery to the buyer.

  NO, the revenue should be recorded when products are sold by the recipient
  (consignee), i.e. transfer of risks. If the goods are not sold, they will be returned to
  the seller and hence no profit should be recognized.




ESSEC                                                                                        5

Pre-Msc Accounting CPTC 31081

Amorti – Solution


Term T1 2026-2027
Amorti – Exercise
A company is considering investing in a project with a five-year useful life. The project involves paying €75 000 for a
licence to manufacture a new product and equipping a production line at a cost of €300 000. In order to launch the
product the company plans a three-month advertising campaign which will cost €100 000.
Assuming that in each year the expected sales are €1 000 000 and expenses other than those detailed above are
€800 000, draw up two alternative series of income statements for the project in the first two years of use, by
using (a) the straight-line method, and (b) the diminishing balance method at 40 per cent per annum, for the
production line. In both sets, decide whether the licence and the advertising campaign should be recognized as
assets or as expenses, and treat them identically in the two sets.

                                             2. Montvert1

                                               Break-even
                                      Cost-volume-profit analysis
                                               10 minutes




A mid-sized manufacturer of pens, Montvert, learned about your competencies in cost management
and management control.

Montvert manufactures and sells pens. In 2024, sales revenues were 20 millions euros. Given the
high-quality of its products, Montvert is able to sell its pens at 2€ per unit.

Montvert’s owner and director general asks you for your help in further analyzing the economic
situation of the firm:

1. What is the present operating profit? What is the break-even point in sales? In revenues?

2. Calculate the new operating profit and the new break-even point in sales for each of the
following changes (consider them as independent questions):

a. An increase in raw material cost will increase by €0.16 the unit variable cost.

b. An advertising campaign would increase fixed costs by €360,000 but could also increase sales
volume by 10 percent.

c. A promotional sale (a 20 percent discount on the usual selling price) could increase sales output
by 40 percent and decrease variable costs by 10 percent.

d. A higher-end positioning of the product would allow raising sales prices by 10 percent yet would
equally increase fixed costs by about €80,000.



To help you in your analysis, she provides you with some additional information on the cost situation:
according to her records, annual fixed costs amount €3,600,000 and variable costs per unit are €1.20.

                                          3. WALK-ABOUT2

                                Cost-Volume-Profit relationships, break-even
                                               Intermediate level
                                                  30 minutes

Walk-About Ltd operates a chain of shoe stores. The stores sell ten different styles of inexpensive
men’s shoes with identical unit costs and selling prices. A unit is defined as a pair of shoes. Each
store has a store manager who is paid a fixed salary. Individual salespeople receive a fixed salary and
a sales commission. Walk-About is trying to determine the desirability of opening another store,
which is expected to have the following revenue and cost relationships:

    Selling price per unit                             £ 30.00

    Sales commission                                   5%

    Cost of shoes                                      £ 19.50

    Annual Rent                                        £ 60 000

    Annual cost of salaries                            £ 200 000

    Advertising                                        £ 80 000

    Other fixed costs                                  £ 20 000


QUESTIONS

Consider each question independently
      1. What is the annual breakeven in units sold, in revenues? If 35,000 units are sold, what will be
         the store’s operating profit or loss?
      2. If the store managers were paid £ 0.30 per unit sold in addition to their current fixed salary,
         what would be the annual breakeven point in units sold? In revenue?
      3. Refer to the original data. If sales commissions were discontinued for individual salespeople
         in favor of an £ 81,000 increase in fixed salaries,
              a. what would be the annual breakeven in units sold? In revenues?
              b. Calculate the number of units sold where the operating profit would be equal under
                 (a) a fixed-salary plan;
                 (b) the lower fixed-salary and a commission plan of 5% (for salespeople only).
              c. Calculate the operating profit or loss for each plan (a and b) at sales level of
                 i. 50,000 sales units; ii. 60,000 sales units.
              d. Suppose the target operating profit is £ 168,000. How many units must be sold to reach
                 the target number under each salary plan (a and b) ?


2

                                      5. Immoservices

                                          Job-costing systems
                                               Basic level
                                               15 minutes

Immoservices is a recently formed services company, specialized in real estate management
consultancy for small and medium-size firms. On the last period, Immoservices had two clients,
Pemberley inc. and Netherfield Ltd.
Mrs Elizabeth Bennet, the managing partner of Immoservices, has just finished a tense telephone call
with Mr Darcy, President of Pemberley. Mr Darcy complained about the price Immoservices charged
for some survey completed for Pemberley (conveyancing and lease transfer). He requested a
breakdown of the charges. He also indicated that a competing firm has contacted him and that
Immoservices would be challenged and would have to bid for a lease transfer job next month. Mr
Darcy ended the call by saying that if Immoservices would bid a price similar to the one charged this
month, Immoservices would not be hired for next month’s job.
Mrs Bennet is dismayed by the telephone call. She is also puzzled because she believes that
Immoservices has much expertise and is highly efficient in lease transfer. The Darcy’s telephone call
is the bad news of the week. The good news is that yesterday Mrs Racine received an e-mail from
Immoservices’ other client, Mr Bingley from Netherfield Ltd, saying that they were very pleased
woth both the quality and the price charged on its most recent survey.
Mrs Bennet decides to collect data on the Pemberley and Netherfield cases. Immoservices uses a cost-
based approach to billing each case, pricing the cost of the case plus 30% mark-up. Currently, it uses
a single direct-cost category, for professional labor time, and a single indirect-cost pool: general
support. Indirect costs are allocated to cases on the basis of professional labor-hours per cases. The
cases files show the following:

                                   Pemberley                         Netherfield

 Professional labor time           104 hours                         96 hours

Professional labor time costs £70 an hour. Total indirect costs for the last period were £21,000.


QUESTIONS

1. Why is it important for Immoservices to understand the costs associated with individual cases?
Present an overview diagram of the existing job-costing system.
2.   Calculate the cost of the Pemberley and Netherfield cases.
3. With the view to improve Immoservices’ cost-pricing system, Mrs Bennet would like to split
the general support pool in two pools. An analysis of the overhead costs shows that administrative
costs amounts £7,000, and Reference costs (for subscription to databases, surveys and reviews)
amounts to £14,000. Administrative costs are now grouped in a pool called Administration. The cost
driver is the professional labor time. Reference costs are grouped in a second pool and the cost driver
is the number of requests made to the library. Pemberly case needed 2 requests, Netherfield needed
8 requests. What would have been the cost and the billing of these cases with the new system?

                                            6. Alp’Ski

                                         Indirect cost allocation
                                           Intermediate level
                                               30 minutes

ALP’SKI manufactures two types of “special” high-end skis: GRIMPER and EXTREME. The
GRIMPER is a product more complex to assemble (it is made of a wooden core, a thin aluminium
foil and its side are reinforced with carbon fiber). However, it is made of cheaper raw material. It is
a high value-added product, delivered in small quantities to a large number of customers (most of
them sport oriented retail outlets). The EXTREME ski is made of wood, glass resin and carbon fibre.
Raw materials for this product are more expensive. EXTREME has a more concentrated customer
base.
2023 sales were the following:
GRIMPER ski sales: €400,000 (800 pairs of skis, at €500 /pair)
EXTREME ski sales: €420,000 (210 pairs of skis, at €2,000 / pair).


Each product has its own direct costs:

           Direct costs (in euros)                   GRIMPER                            EXTREME

Raw material used                                                     80,000                          220,000

Direct labor (variable)

       Direct labor Cutting Workshop          500 h x 40€/h =         20,000       500 h x 40€/h =     20,000
      Direct labor Assembly Workshop        2,000 h x 40€/h =         80,000       500 h x 40€/h =     20,000

(Hours x hourly rate)                    2,500 h x 40€/h =          100,000    1,000 h x 40€/h =     40,000

Other direct costs (fixed)                                          70,000                           40,000

        TOTAL DIRECT COSTS                                          250,000                          300,000



During the same period, other costs are incurred. These are the indirect costs of the products. They
are mostly fixed costs.
  -     Cutting Workshop costs                 35,000
  -     Assembly Workshop costs                45,000
  -     Information Systems (IS) Costs         60,000
  -     Purchasing costs                       25,000
  -     Maintenance costs                      50,000
        TOTAL INDIRECT COSTS                  215,000

                           Cutting        Assembly            IS       Purchasing       Maintenance
                          Workshop        workshop

 IS                          40%             60%            - 100%

 Purchasing                  40%             60%              -          - 100%
Cutting workshop pool costs are allocated on products on the basis of K€ of raw materials. Assembly
workshop pool costs are allocated on the basis of the assembly workshop direct labor hours.


Required : Calculate the cost of each type of ski (the total amount and cost per ski)

                                           7. McCarthy

                                               ABC method
                                            Intermediary level
                                                20 minutes

McCarthy potatoes produces and sells frozen fries at its Armentieres’ factory. It has been dedicated
to retail market only. The reputation of McCarthy potatoes was excellent. Recently the company
entered the business-to-business market by selling to collective kitchens (hospitals, university
restaurants, in-firm restaurants). However, its break in this market has been slower than expected.
The current management accounting system proposes only one direct charge account, raw materials,
corresponding to the purchase of potatoes. There is only one pool comprising all the other costs, «
production support ». These costs are allocated to the products on the basis of the kilogram of
potatoes. The management accounting system does not distinguish between retail and business
products.
In 2024, the company will have produced 1,000,000 kg of frozen fries: 900,000 kg for the retail
market, and 100,000 kg for the business market. The total amount of charges follows:
Purchase of potatoes: € 150,000
Production support: € 983,000

Question 1 : Calculate the cost of production for one kilo of frozen fries.

Late 2024, McCarthy potatoes answered a call for tender in the business market, but its proposal has
been rejected as it was 30% more expensive than the competitor’s selected. This was all the more
deceiving and striking for McCarthy potatoes than the margin calculated was particularly low and
that Armentieres factory is reputed for being the most efficient in the industry.
The CEO of McCarthy potatoes wants to improve its production cost system by distinguishing the
production costs for the retail market from those for the business market.
First, it was acknowledged that €188,000 over the € 983,000 production support costs were packaging
costs that could be directly allocated to the product types: €180,000 for the retail market and € 8,000
for the business market. From now they will be considered as direct costs.
Second, as the need for potatoes is the same for retail market fries and business market fries, the
remaining production support costs will still be allocated on the basis of kg of potatoes.

Question 2 : Calculate the cost of one kilo of fries for the retail market and for the business market.

The trainee of the company suggests improving the cost system by analyzing the activities involved
in the production support pool. In her survey she identifies the relevant activities, the amount of costs
for each activity and the application base / cost driver to use for each activity: three activities has been
determined: washing, cutting and packaging.




                                                -9-


 Activity                                  Cost

 Washing                              € 120,000

 Cutting                              € 231,000

 Packaging                            € 444,000


Washing: there is no difference between the potatoes for the retail market or the business market
here. The application base / cost driver is the kg of potatoes.
Cutting : the process is different for the retail market and the business market fries. The cutting
machines operate (a) 250 kg of potatoes per hour for the retail market ; (b) 400 kg of potatoes per
hour for the business market. The application base / cost driver is the hour of cutting process.
Packaging : the packaging process is different for the retail market and the business market fries.
The packaging machines operates: (a) 25 kg of fries per hour for the retail market ; (b) 100 kg of
potatoes per hour for the business market. The application base / cost driver is the hour of packaging
process.

Question 3 :

a°) Calculate the cost of a unit of application / cost driver for each of the three activities.
b°) Calculate the cost of a kilogram fries for the retail market and for the business market with this
new cost system.
c°) How could the McCarthy potatoes management could use this information system ?

                                           9. Puyricard

                                   Cost allocation – relevant costs
                                           Advanced level
                                             45 minutes


Puyricard is one of main French premium chocolate-maker and confectionary. Based in Vaucluse,
the company makes three types of products: chocolates, candied chestnuts and fruit pastes. Products
are sold in Puyricard stores, either in Paris or in the rest of France. The company also has an internet
site which sends products all over the world.




The management team is currently analyzing contributions (raw margins on variable production costs,
net margin on variable and fixed production costs), full costs and profits for each type of products.
The company has a cost accounting system based on cost pools, and each of these pools corresponds
to the main departments of the company.
For 2025, sales are expected as follows:
                                  Selling price per Kg         Volumes produced and sold (Kg)

         Chocolate                         55                               70,000

     Candied Chesnut                       70                               10,000

         Fruit paste                       35                               40,000




For 2025, direct costs are expected as follows:

- Costs of raw products: 14€ / kg for chocolates; 7€ / kg for candied chestnut; 3€ / kg for fruit paste;
- Costs of direct labour: one hour of labour is needed for each kg of chocolate. The production of
candied chestnut requires more work, because more supervision is needed and each package has to
be prepared manually. Thus, labour time is 2 hours for each kg of marron glacé. Finally, fruit paste
needs only half an hour for each kg. Hourly labour cost (including all social costs) is 16 euros per
hour.
- Other direct (and fixed) costs (mainly the machine depreciation) are expected to be 30,000€ for
chocolates; 15,000€ for candied chestnut; 10,000 € for fruit paste.
Other costs are considered in the following centers:

                                                - 13 -


- Information Systems department budgets 300,000 € costs. These costs are recorded in the same pool
and then distributed 40 % to the Manufacturing shop and 60 % to the Facilities department. These
costs are then added to the following pools:


- The manufacturing shop targets costs of 584,000 € for 2025 (mostly indirect work, depreciations
and costs of machines). In order to allocate these costs to products, the allocation unit is K€ of direct
labour;
-The Facilities department, in charge of the quality process, logistics, maintenance of the factury. The
allocation unit is K€ of sales. The department targets costs of 1,486,000 € for 2025.



Questions:

1. Prepare the 2025 budget. Calculate the raw and net margins expected for each product line, and the
total cost and total cost per kg for each product, by allocating the indirect costs following the
company’s costing system.
2. Propose some performance indicators and calculate them for each product.
3. The managing director meets with the production manager, the sales manager and the financial
director. Given the poor performance of candied chestnut, they consider three alternatives:
Option A: stop producing candied chestnut. In this hypothesis, direct costs of production would be
eliminated, and indirect costs would decrease from 584,000 € to 500,000 euros. However, commercial
indirect costs and general services costs would remain the same. They have no idea of the impact of
stopping candied chestnut on the rest of the sales.
Option B: the production manager suggests buying a new machine which would improve
manufacturing costs of candied chestnut. (This machine would be added to the other existing
machines). The cost of raw material would be 6 euros per kilo and the company would save 10 % of
working time. Depreciation of the machine would amount to 10 000 euros/year.
Option C: the sales manager received a call from a large network of work councils, proposing services
and special offers to the employees of French companies subscribing to the network. This network
suggests including Puyricard candied chestnut on its Christmas catalog if a 30 % discount is offered.
The sales manager estimates that sales could reach 3,000 kg per year. Current production structure
would be able to manage this surplus activity and there would be no additional administrative costs.

Analyze each of these options and their possible combinations, both from a financial and strategic
point of view. Which proposition/s would you suggest to the company to adopt? Why?




                                              - 14 -
